lectures.title: Assessing the Transatlantic Relationship — Realism, Liberalism, Idealism

sections.title: I. Introduction: Europe and America as a Strategic Pair
sections.html:
The transatlantic relationship — the political, economic, military, and ideological relationship between the United States and Europe — is foundational to post-1945 international order. But its origins go much deeper, rooted in:

  • Europe’s role as the civilizational “core” from which U.S. political ideals emerged
  • America’s identity as both part of Europe (culturally) and separate from it (geographically and strategically)
  • Competing intellectual traditions in U.S. foreign policy: Realism, Liberalism, and Idealism Lecture 1 sets the conceptual foundation for understanding why the U.S. related to Europe in such distinctive ways, long before NATO or the Marshall Plan. These deep historical patterns are essential for interpreting American grand strategy in later lectures.

sections.title: II. The U.S. and Europe: Interconnected but Separate
sections.html:
The early slides visually depict:

The US and Europe

America saw itself simultaneously as:

  • a European offshoot (culturally, politically, ideologically),
  • but also as physically separate and therefore able to remain detached from Europe’s power struggles.

The phrase “America – off-shore Europe” captures this dual identity.

The U.S. inherited European institutions — especially British liberal political traditions — yet believed its distance allowed it to avoid the corruption, war, and rivalries that plagued the European continent.

This duality explains why American policy toward Europe oscillated between:

  • engagement (supporting allies, shaping international order), and
  • withdrawal (steering clear of entanglements).

sections.title: III. America’s Intellectual Traditions in Foreign Policy
sections.html:
The lecture frames U.S. foreign policy as a struggle between Realism and Idealism, with Liberalism as a hybrid tradition.

1. Idealism

Idealism holds that American foreign policy should:

  • promote democracy, liberty, and self-determination
  • spread American political values abroad
  • view international relations as moral struggle
  • emphasize cooperation, peace, and rule-based order

This tradition comes from:

  • Puritan moral mission,
  • Jeffersonian universalism,
  • Wilson’s Fourteen Points,
  • belief in the U.S. as a model for humanity.

Under Idealism, America is a city upon a hill — a morally exceptional power with a responsibility to “lead by example.”

2. Realism

Realism emphasizes:

  • national interest
  • security and survival
  • balance of power
  • military and economic capabilities
  • engagement only when vital interests are at stake

This tradition sees Europe not primarily as a community of values, but as:

  • a zone of potential threats,
  • a region in which hostile hegemons (Napoleon, Kaiser, Hitler, Stalin) could destabilize global balance of power.

3. Liberalism

Liberalism blends idealism (values) with realism (institutions):

  • supports international cooperation through rules
  • promotes free trade and open markets
  • strengthens international institutions (League of Nations, UN, NATO)
  • believes that democracies are more peaceful and cooperative

This is the intellectual backbone of the post-1945 transatlantic order.

sections.title: IV. George Washington’s Farewell Address: The Foundational Doctrine of American Isolationism
sections.html:
Washington famously warned:

“Steer clear of permanent alliances with any portion of the foreign world.”

This was not a call for isolation from trade or diplomacy — but from entangling military and political commitments in Europe.

Why Washington said this:

1. The U.S. was weak, newly independent, and geographically distant.

2. European politics were dominated by great power rivalries that could entrap the U.S. in unwanted wars.

3. America believed it could remain peaceful and prosperous by focusing on internal development.

4. The U.S. wanted to avoid being drawn into Europe’s “ambition, rivalship, humor, or caprice.”

This became the guiding doctrine of American foreign policy for over a century.

sections.title: V. Nineteenth-Century Expansion & U.S. Rise to Global Relevance
sections.html:
The presentation includes charts from Paul Kennedy showing relative manufacturing output and national income.

These illustrate how the material foundations of American power changed dramatically from 1750 to 1914.

1. Early U.S.: Marginal power

  • In 1750 → insignificant industrial output
  • In 1800 → still peripheral compared to Europe
  • U.S. wealth and power remained regional, not global

2. Industrial Revolution transforms the United States

By late 19th century, the U.S. underwent explosive industrialization:

  • Rapid expansion of factories, railroads, steel production
  • Huge population growth
  • Westward expansion
  • Rise of American corporations

3. By 1900, America rivaled the great powers

According to Kennedy’s data:

  • U.S. manufacturing surpassed every European country
  • By 1914, U.S. GNP exceeded Germany + Britain combined
  • U.S. naval power rose dramatically (3rd largest by 1914)

Why this matters:

This economic transformation set the stage for:

  • global engagement
  • overseas expansion
  • the shift from isolation toward involvement in Europe
  • the later ability to rescue Europe in two world wars
  • and eventually to lead the transatlantic order

sections.title: VI. The Spanish-American War as Watershed (1898)
sections.html:
The Spanish-American War marks America’s first major overseas military intervention and the beginning of its global strategic presence.

The USS Maine exploded and sank in Havana Harbor on February 15, 1898, killing 268 sailors and igniting public outrage that led to the Spanish-American War. While an initial U.S. Naval Court of Inquiry concluded a mine caused the explosion, the exact cause remains debated.

Manila bay

Key consequences:

  • U.S. took control of former Spanish colonies (Philippines, Guam, Puerto Rico)
  • Annexation of Hawaii
  • U.S. became a naval power and acquired Pacific and Caribbean bases
  • Marked a break with strict Washingtonian isolationism

Underlying factors:

  • Economic interests (markets, trade routes)
  • Strategic interests (naval bases for Mahanian sea power doctrine)
  • Ideological justifications (liberation, civilization, democracy)
  • Domestic pressures (expansionist sentiment)

This war marks the beginning of “Rise to Globalism.”

sections.title: VII. World War I: Idealism Meets Harsh Reality
sections.html:
Slides show The First World War twice — emphasizing its profound impact.

1. U.S. entry (1917)

After years of neutrality, the U.S. intervened due to:

  • German unrestricted submarine warfare
  • Zimmermann Telegram
  • Economic ties to Britain and France
  • Belief that German victory would threaten global order
  • Wilson’s idealism (making the world “safe for democracy”)

2. Wilson’s Idealism and the League of Nations

Wilson proposed:

  • collective security
  • self-determination
  • international law
  • ending power politics

3. U.S. Senate rejects the League

This marked a return to isolationism.

Why?

  • Fear of entanglements in Europe
  • Preservation of congressional power to declare war
  • Resentment of European imperialism and alliances
  • Domestic political divisions

Consequences:

  • Europe rebuilt an unstable order
  • Lack of U.S. engagement contributed to interwar instability
  • Depression, fascism, and rising authoritarian powers grew unchecked

This failure profoundly shaped U.S. behavior after WWII.

sections.title: VIII. The Interwar Period: Retreat, Disillusionment, Disaster
sections.html:
The presentation ends with a single slide: Interwar period.

This period was dominated by:

1. American retreat

  • U.S. rejected League of Nations
  • Passed Neutrality Acts to avoid war
  • Focused on domestic economic recovery (New Deal)

2. European fragmentation and crisis

  • Rise of fascism in Germany, Italy, Spain
  • Weakened democracies
  • Economic collapse and mass unemployment
  • Breakdown of Versailles settlement

3. U.S. misperception

Americans believed they could remain detached from Europe, even as global threats escalated.

4. Strategic blindness

The U.S. underestimated:

  • how global economic collapse destabilizes politics
  • how authoritarian regimes exploit power vacuums
  • how isolationism can enable aggression

Lessons from this failure later shaped post-1945 American grand strategy, which rejected isolation and embraced:

  • international institutions
  • collective security
  • European reconstruction
  • permanent alliances (NATO)

sections.title: IX. Bringing Realism, Liberalism, Idealism Together: How These Traditions Frame the Transatlantic Relationship
sections.html:
This lecture equips you with the intellectual toolkit needed to analyze U.S.–Europe relations across the whole course.

1. Realism explains:

  • U.S. intervention in two world wars
  • containment of Soviet Union
  • military alliances (NATO)
  • balance of power logic
  • strategic importance of Europe

2. Liberalism explains:

  • Marshall Plan
  • support for European integration
  • establishment of UN, IMF, World Bank
  • economic interdependence as peace strategy

3. Idealism explains:

  • American support for democracy
  • Wilsonian rhetoric
  • human rights and self-determination
  • moral framing of foreign policy
  • U.S. belief in exceptionalism

Together, these traditions explain:

  • why the U.S. is simultaneously pragmatic and moralistic
  • why it promotes both power and principles
  • why Europe is both a partner and an object of American strategy
  • why the transatlantic relationship is durable, despite occasional crises

sections.title: X. Conclusion: The Deep Roots of the Transatlantic Relationship
sections.html:
This lecture emphasizes that the transatlantic relationship is not accidental or merely post-1945. It is built on:

  • shared cultural and ideological origins
  • historical patterns of U.S. isolation and selective engagement
  • strategic shifts driven by industrial power and global threats
  • competing U.S. foreign policy traditions
  • Europe’s role as both model and potential danger
  • recurring cycles of war, retreat, and renewed involvement

Understanding these foundations is essential before examining WWII, the Marshall Plan, NATO, and the Cold War — because those developments emerged directly from the patterns established here.

lectures.title: World War II and American Grand Strategy

sections.title: I. Introduction: Why this topic matters
sections.html:
The Second World War fundamentally transformed America’s role in world politics, Europe’s political landscape, and the foundations of the transatlantic relationship. What makes this transformation unique is that the United States emerged from WWII not simply as a victorious power, but as a system-shaping superpower with:

  • unprecedented material capabilities,
  • a global network of military positions,
  • ideological confidence, and
  • a strategic vision for Europe that combined power, values, and institutions.

This period marks the birth of American grand strategy toward Europe, which would evolve into an integrated economic, political, and military project including the Marshall Plan, NATO, postwar occupation policies, and support for European integration.

The slides give the core points. The readings (Lundestad, Cox & Kennedy-Pipe, Sloan) provide deeper insight into whythe U.S. acted the way it did, what strategic thinking lay behind it, and how this shaped the Cold War international order.

sections.title: II. America Before the War: Isolationism, Caution, and Moral Framing
sections.html:
1. U.S. and the Outbreak of War

When World War II broke out in September 1939, the United States did not immediately join. This reflected:

  • Domestic political constraints — after WWI, Americans were hostile to foreign entanglements.
  • The Neutrality Acts — legally restricted U.S. involvement.
  • Economic concerns — the Great Depression made foreign conflicts seem remote and unaffordable.
  • Geographic distance — Americans believed oceans shielded the country from European turmoil.

This was a society determined to avoid another catastrophic war. Yet Roosevelt understood earlier than most that the U.S. could not stay indifferent to events in Europe.

2. FDR’s Fireside Chat, 3 September 1939

FDR famously said he could not ask Americans to remain “neutral in thought as well,” acknowledging publicly that total neutrality was impossible in a moral confrontation between democracy and fascism.

Elaboration:

This speech is a turning point because Roosevelt reframed neutrality:

  • Not as moral indifference,
  • but as an ethical stance compatible with supporting victims of aggression.

This allowed him to prepare public opinion gradually. He needed Americans to accept the idea that their security was tied to events in Europe. This was essential for legitimizing Lend-Lease later on.

3. Churchill’s Appeal (June 1940)

Churchill’s famous “We shall fight on the beaches…” speech included a direct message to the U.S.: that Britain would continue fighting until, “in God’s good time, the New World… steps forth to the rescue of the Old”.

Elaboration:

Churchill strategically framed the American role as historically destined. Britain’s survival hinged on U.S. assistance. His rhetoric established a moral obligation for America to save European civilization — a framing Roosevelt agreed with but had to introduce slowly to the American public.

sections.title: III. The Road to War: From Neutrality to Global Power
sections.html:
1. The Atlantic Charter (August 1941)

This joint declaration by Roosevelt and Churchill defined shared war aims:

  • No territorial aggrandizement
  • Self-determination
  • Free trade
  • Collective security (proto-UN)

Importance:

It foreshadowed the liberal world order the U.S. would create after 1945. The Charter represented the ideological heart of U.S. grand strategy: combining American values with strategic interests.

2. Pearl Harbor (7 December 1941)

Japan’s attack forced immediate U.S. entry into the war. Roosevelt declared the date “a day of infamy.” Germany declared war on the U.S. in solidarity with Japan.

Why this changed everything:

  • It united American public opinion behind war.
  • It ended decades of isolationist politics.
  • It legitimized enormous military mobilization.
  • It provided a mandate for global engagement.

In short: Pearl Harbor launched the U.S. into the role of global superpower.

3. “Mixture of Idealism and Realism” in U.S. Foreign Policy

The presentation highlights the dual nature of U.S. policy:

Idealism:

  • The U.S. viewed itself as a different, morally motivated power.
  • It believed in democracy, open trade, self-determination.

Realism:

  • American security required preventing any hostile hegemon from dominating Europe or Asia.
  • Maintaining balance of power and protecting access to markets were vital.

Synthesis:

American grand strategy always combined values (democracy, open markets) with interests (security, power). This blend defines the transatlantic relationship.

sections.title: IV. Wartime Cooperation and Emerging Power Shifts
sections.html:
1. The U.S. as Junior Partner (1942–1944)

  • Britain had more experience and intelligence assets.
  • Washington deferred to British strategy (North Africa first).
  • U.S. forces were still building capacity.

But: the U.S. was out-producing all other powers combined. By 1943, American troops, supplies, and factories were sustaining the Allied war effort.

2. The U.S. as Senior Partner (1944–1945)

By D-Day (June 1944):

  • U.S. forces were numerically dominant.
  • American commanders (Eisenhower) were leading major operations.
  • U.S. industrial output dwarfed all others.

Significance:

This shift was not merely military — it set the stage for the U.S. to lead postwar reconstruction, occupation, and institution building.

sections.title: V. The U.S. in 1945: Emergence of a Global Superpower
sections.html:
The slide notes astonishing facts about U.S. strength:

  • Two-thirds of world industrial production
  • Half the world’s wealth
  • World’s largest navy
  • Occupying Japan and much of Germany
  • Possessing the atomic bomb

This was the most concentrated accumulation of power in modern history.

Why these numbers matter:

  • Europe was devastated; the U.S. was enriched.
  • The U.S. had unmatched capacity to shape international rules.
  • American leaders believed they had responsibility to prevent future catastrophes.

Enter bipolarity

The Soviet Union, despite winning on the Eastern Front, was economically shattered but militarily dominant in Eastern Europe.

Thus, the postwar world became bipolar—a U.S.-centered West vs. a Soviet-controlled East.

sections.title: VI. The Soviet Problem: Territorial Control and Ideological Expansion
sections.html:
Stalin’s view:

“Whoever occupies territory imposes his own social system”.

Consequences:

  • Soviet armies’ presence in Eastern Europe translated into communist control.
  • This created direct geopolitical and ideological confrontation with the U.S.

This tension began even before the war ended, shaping negotiations at Yalta and Potsdam.

sections.title: VII. Yalta and Potsdam: Managing Victory, Sowing Division
sections.html:
1. Yalta (February 1945)

The Big Three attempted to balance three goals:

  • Punish Nazi Germany
  • Establish democratic governments
  • Maintain alliance unity

But issues arose:

  • The definition of “free elections” varied.
  • Stalin insisted on friendly governments for Soviet security.
  • Roosevelt needed Soviet entry into the Pacific war and cooperation in the UN.

2. Potsdam (July–August 1945)

By Potsdam:

  • Roosevelt had died; Truman took a tougher stance.
  • Churchill was replaced by Attlee.
  • Trust in Stalin declined.

Sticking points:

  • Germany’s future
  • Poland’s borders
  • Reparations
  • Fate of Eastern Europe

3. Why administering liberated countries became problematic

The slide’s question is central:

Why was post-liberation administration so contentious?

Deep explanation:

  • The Soviet Union imposed communist regimes in territories it liberated (reflecting Stalin’s security doctrine).
  • The U.S. and Britain expected democratic self-determination.
  • These visions were incompatible.
  • Military control on the ground determined political outcomes.

This made postwar cooperation nearly impossible and directly fed into the division of Europe.

sections.title: VIII. Linking the End of WWII to American Grand Strategy (reading integration)
sections.html:
This is where the readings add vital depth.

A. The Marshall Plan and Economic Strategy (Cox & Kennedy-Pipe)

Cox & Kennedy-Pipe emphasize that:

1. The Marshall Plan was multipurpose

It aimed to:

  • Rebuild Western Europe
  • Prevent communist political gains
  • Reconcile France and Germany
  • Promote economic integration
  • Export elements of the American economic model

The U.S. believed European economic health was essential to:

  • World stability
  • U.S. prosperity
  • Containment of the USSR

2. Not purely benevolent

Revisionist and post-revisionist scholars note:

  • The Plan was partly responsible for institutionalizing the East–West divide.
  • Earlier or longer openness toward Soviet participation might have altered Cold War dynamics.
  • The U.S., intentionally or not, solidified a Western bloc and pushed the USSR to lock down Eastern Europe more tightly.

3. Why the Plan was revolutionary

It represented:

  • The first large-scale U.S. peacetime intervention in European domestic affairs.
  • A shift from isolation to active global leadership.
  • Foundations for European integration through the OEEC.

B. NATO and the Transatlantic Bargain (Sloan)

Sloan explains that the creation of NATO (1949) formed the military cornerstone of American grand strategy.

1. The Transatlantic Bargain

The unwritten deal was:

  • The U.S. provides military protection, nuclear guarantees, and troops stationed in Europe.
  • Europe accepts U.S. leadership, alignment against the USSR, and integration into a U.S.-led security system.

This arrangement stabilized Western Europe and institutionalized America’s role.

2. Why NATO was essential for the U.S.

  • Prevented Soviet expansion
  • Ensured no revival of German militarism
  • Kept the U.S. engaged in European affairs
  • Gave the U.S. strategic forward bases
  • Linked Europe’s future to American power

3. Why Europe needed NATO

  • Europe was too weak to defend itself.
  • The U.S. nuclear umbrella compensated for Soviet conventional superiority.
  • NATO provided a mechanism for German rearmament within constraints.

4. NATO’s institutional uniqueness

NATO created:

  • Permanent command structures
  • A coordinated defense policy
  • An integrated military system
  • A political forum for continuous US-Europe consultation

This institutionalization of American leadership ensured that U.S. influence became embedded, not temporary.

C. “Empire by Integration”: Political Strategy (Lundestad)

Lundestad argues the U.S. created a unique form of empire — not by conquest, but by promoting European integrationon terms compatible with American leadership.

1. Five motives behind U.S. support for European integration

Lundestad identifies five clusters, from least to most important:

1. The American model
– Federalism, free markets, democracy as universalizable ideals.
– U.S. leaders believed Europe should follow the American example.
– E.g., 1947 resolution proposing a “United States of Europe.”

2. A more rational, efficient Europe
– Integration would reduce destructive nationalism.
– It would simplify U.S.–Europe negotiations.
– As Eisenhower said, united Europe “would produce miracles” economically.

3. Reducing the American burden
– Europe should eventually share security responsibilities.
– This did not happen quickly, but the motive persisted (e.g., EDC, later the EU).

4. Containing the Soviet Union
– A unified Europe was a stronger barrier to communism.
– Western unity reinforced NATO and the Marshall Plan.
– U.S. leaders even hoped integration might “attract” Eastern European states away from the USSR.

5. Containing Germany (most important)
– Germany needed to be strong but controlled.
– Integration “bound” Germany to the West politically and economically.
– This concern resurfaced after German reunification in 1990.

2. Integration was never meant to replace the U.S.

The U.S. supported European unity only within an Atlantic framework.

It opposed any form of Europe as an independent “third force” neutral between Washington and Moscow.

3. Combining influence and partnership

The U.S. held extraordinary power (NATO, trade system, cultural influence), but much of Europe welcomed this because it ensured:

  • Security
  • Economic recovery
  • Reconciliation between old rivals
  • Political stability

Thus, Europe voluntarily entered an American-led order. This is why Lundestad calls it an “empire by invitation.”

sections.title: IX. Bringing It All Together: WWII as the Origin of American Grand Strategy
sections.html:
World War II produced the fundamental conditions for American grand strategy:

1. Material dominance

Without WWII’s destruction of Europe, no U.S.-led reconstruction would have been possible.

2. Ideological clarity

The war against fascism reinforced:

  • Democracy
  • Collective security
  • Anti-totalitarianism

These became building blocks of the postwar order.

3. Geopolitical confrontation

Soviet expansion forced the U.S. to construct a cohesive Western bloc.

4. Institutional innovation

The war created both the necessity and the opportunity for:

  • The United Nations
  • Bretton Woods institutions
  • Marshall Plan
  • NATO
  • OEEC → EEC → EU

5. Leadership acceptance

Unlike after WWI, Europe now wanted American leadership.

The “empire by invitation” dynamic emerged because Europe understood the alternatives:

  • devastation
  • Soviet domination
  • return to violent nationalism

6. A permanent U.S. role in Europe

American leaders concluded that:

  • European security was inseparable from American security.
  • Geographic distance no longer ensured safety.
  • Withdrawal would invite disaster.

This became a foundational principle of American grand strategy and of the transatlantic relationship.

sections.title: X. Conclusion: What WWII Ultimately Meant for Transatlantic Relations
sections.html:
World War II forged a new world order, in which:

  • The U.S. became the indispensable Western power.
  • Europe was rebuilt within a U.S.-led framework.
  • A bipolar U.S.–Soviet rivalry defined global politics.
  • Institutions bound Europe and America together.
  • American grand strategy focused on preventing hostile dominance of Europe, integrating Germany, containing the USSR, and building open markets.

This was the birth of a long-lasting transatlantic community, anchored in shared interests, shared values, and shared institutions — a community that began in the darkest days of WWII and evolved into NATO, the EU, and the broader liberal international order.

lectures.title: The origins of the Cold War and the US engagement in European affairs

sections.title: I. Introduction: The Meaning of 1945–1950 in Transatlantic Relations
sections.html:
This period marks the moment when the United States — historically isolationist and skeptical of permanent alliances — permanently abandoned disengagement and instead became the guarantor of Western European security, committed economically, politically, and militarily.

Between 1945 and 1950, the foundations of the Cold War were laid in Europe; the U.S. moved from:

  • wanting to demobilize and withdraw, to
  • leading an unprecedented Western alliance and launching the Marshall Plan, to
  • creating NATO and endorsing a long-term military commitment.

This transformation was not inevitable. The lecture shows that U.S. policy after WWII was shaped by fear of Soviet expansion, collapse of wartime cooperation, and growing awareness that a stable Europe was essential to U.S. global interests. The readings expand this by showing how:

  • Truman’s worldview and domestic pressures shaped early Cold War choices (Offner)
  • Economic reconstruction became the major tool of strategy (Cox & Kennedy-Pipe)
  • U.S. support for European integration began as a security strategy (Lundestad)
  • NATO institutionalized the American-led security system (Sloan)

sections.title: II. The U.S. in 1945: From War to Uncertainty
sections.html:
The slide “The US in 1945” sets the starting context:

1. The United States was the strongest power in the world

  • Possessed half the world’s wealth
  • Two-thirds of global industrial production
  • Atomic monopoly
  • Military presence in Europe and Asia

Yet this overwhelming strength did not mean American policymakers wanted to remain in Europe.

2. Strategic ambiguity

The U.S. had three competing impulses:

1. Return to isolationism
– Congress and public wanted immediate demobilization.
– “Bring the boys home” was a powerful domestic demand.

2. Cooperate with the USSR in managing postwar peace
– The wartime alliance had not yet fully collapsed.
– Hopes existed at Yalta and Potsdam for joint administration.

3. Fear of a postwar vacuum
– Europe was devastated; without U.S. support it could slide into instability or fall under Soviet influence.

This mixture of desires and fears created the contradictory mindset of the early Truman administration — a key point developed by Offner, who argues Truman’s early decisions were shaped by lack of clarity, moralistic instincts, and gradual acceptance of confrontation with the Soviet Union.

sections.title: III. Bipolarism and the Postwar Balance
sections.html:
The collapse of Nazi Germany left two superpowers in charge: the U.S. and the Soviet Union. Yet the two were asymmetric in power and security.

1. The Soviet Union: simultaneously strong and weak

The slide summarises:

  • 10% population loss
  • Vast economic destruction
  • But Red Army’s enormous power
  • Occupation of Eastern Europe
  • Victory over the Wehrmacht

This created a geopolitical paradox:

  • militarily dominant in its region,
  • economically devastated,
  • politically insecure,
  • determined to create buffer zones to prevent another invasion.

2. Britain becomes a “junior partner”

  • The British Empire collapsed economically by 1945.
  • Britain could not maintain global commitments.
  • Its decline forced the U.S. to take on greater responsibility.

3. The resulting system: a dangerous bipolarity

  • One superpower economically strong (U.S.)
  • One superpower militarily entrenched in Europe (USSR)
  • Distrust growing rapidly

This tension made Europe the first arena of the Cold War.

sections.title: IV. Yalta and Potsdam: Cooperation Fades
sections.html:
The presentation lists Yalta and Potsdam twice, signaling their centrality.

1. Wartime cooperation conceals deep disagreements

At Yalta (Feb 1945):

  • Agreement on dividing Germany
  • Declaration on liberated Europe
  • Soviets promise free elections
  • Stalin agrees to join UN and war against Japan

At Potsdam (July–Aug 1945):

  • Relations deteriorate
  • Truman adopts tougher line (atomic bomb confidence)
  • No consensus on reparations, Germany’s future, Poland’s borders

2. Why were these conferences important?

They revealed:

  • Contradictory visions
    – U.S. = democracy, open markets
    – USSR = friendly (i.e., controlled) governments in its sphere
  • Mutual suspicion
    – Offner emphasizes Truman’s deep distrust of Stalin, whom he viewed as inherently expansionist.
  • Structural pressures
    – The Red Army’s presence determined political systems in Eastern Europe.

Thus, wartime cooperation turned into postwar confrontation.

sections.title: V. U.S. Attitudes Toward Europe After 1945
sections.html:
American policy was pulled in different directions.

1. Postwar Planning: Europe’s future mattered

American planners viewed Europe as:

  • Essential to global balance
  • A region whose recovery was key to preventing extremist politics
  • The economic center whose collapse had helped cause WWII

Planners wanted a stable, democratic, prosperous Western Europe, but the U.S. had not yet committed to long-term management.

2. Pressures to withdraw

The slide lists strong pressures against involvement:

  • War in the Pacific still ongoing
  • Domestic demand to demobilize (“bring boys home”)
  • Congress dominated by isolationists
  • No one imagined an open-ended commitment

Lundestad notes that in 1945–46 American policy was hesitant; Washington still favored letting Europeans take primary responsibility and hoped for cooperation with the USSR.

Offner reinforces this: Truman initially had no grand strategy for Europe and was preoccupied with Japan, demobilization, and domestic politics.

sections.title: VI. What Changes? The Collapse of Allied Unity (1946–47)
sections.html:
The slide lists Soviet actions that shifted U.S. thinking:

1. Soviet control over Eastern Europe (communist “puppet” governments)

2. Border pressures on Turkey

3. Demand for passage through the Bosporus

4. Support for Greek communists

5. Refusal to withdraw from Iran

6. Stalin’s 1946 speech(maximum rearmament effort in 1946)

7. Perception of a worldwide Soviet conspiracy

Why these mattered:

A. Sovietization of Eastern Europe

  • U.S. saw this as violation of Yalta’s promise of free elections.
  • Poland, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria saw communist takeovers.
  • Reinforced belief USSR was inherently expansionist.

B. Greek Civil War & Turkey (Straits Crisis)

  • Britain could not finance its commitments.
  • U.S. feared Greece and Turkey could fall into Soviet orbit.
  • Core cause of Truman Doctrine.

C. Iran Crisis (1946)

  • Soviets refused to leave northern Iran.
  • First major Cold War confrontation.

D. Stalin’s February 1946 speech

  • Framed conflict as inevitable clash of systems.
  • Reinforced Kennan’s interpretation of communist expansionism.

Offner writes that Truman increasingly saw Soviet actions as part of a global, ideologically driven challenge requiring firmness and resolve.

sections.title: VII. George Kennan and the Logic of Containment
sections.html:
Kennan’s Long Telegram (1946) and “X Article” (1947) shaped U.S. strategy.

Key arguments:

  • Soviet Union is inherently expansionist
  • Motivated by security fears + ideology
  • Can only be stopped by firm containment
  • U.S. must not lose Western Europe, the economic-industrial core of the world
  • Political and economic strength, not war, are the main tools

Kennan argued the U.S. had to provide:

  • Economic aid to prevent collapse
  • Political support to democratic governments
  • Long-term presence to resist Soviet pressure

Lundestad emphasizes that the U.S. saw European stability—and later European integration—as directly linked to containing both the Soviets and Germany.

sections.title: VIII. The Truman Doctrine (12 March 1947)
sections.html:
Truman declared:

“It must be the policy of the United States to support free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation…”

Significance:

1. Ideological framing

The Doctrine turned the Cold War into a global struggle between:

  • Free societies
  • Totalitarian forces

Offner emphasizes that Truman believed in moral confrontation with “evil regimes” and saw communism as a universal threat, reinforcing the doctrinal tone of the speech.

2. Response to British withdrawal

Britain informed the U.S. it could no longer support Greece and Turkey.

This forced the U.S. to take responsibility for preventing communist influence.

3. End of isolationism

For the first time, the U.S. formally committed itself to intervene militarily and financially to stop communist expansion.

This was the true break with 150 years of Washingtonian warnings against alliances.

sections.title: IX. Containment Becomes Practice: From Aid to Intervention
sections.html:
1. The Marshall Plan (June 1947)

Between 1948–51, the U.S. pumped $12.5 billion into Western Europe.

Why the Marshall Plan mattered:

According to Cox & Kennedy-Pipe:

  • It stabilized Western economies
  • Limited communist appeal
  • Encouraged cooperation and integration (OEEC)
  • Marked U.S. leadership of the Western bloc
  • Contributed to Cold War division since Soviets refused participation

Lundestad adds:

  • Marshall Plan was the first major tool of “empire by integration,” encouraging Europeans to cooperate and pushing them toward regional unity under U.S. leadership.

2. Covert Actions: 1948 Italian Election

  • CIA funneled money to anti-communist parties.
  • Demonstrated new willingness to intervene politically in Europe.

3. OEEC and Integration

  • U.S. insisted Europe allocate Marshall Aid collectively.
  • The OEEC became a stepping-stone toward the EEC.

This shows how containment and integration were linked.

sections.title: X. European Security Initiatives (1947–1949)
sections.html:
The lecture lists:

1. Treaty of Dunkirk (1947) — Franco-British defense pact

2. Brussels Pact (1948) — extended to Benelux; early collective defense

3. Vandenberg Resolution (1948) — permitted U.S. to join a peacetime alliance

4. All “augmented” by the Atlantic Alliance (NATO, 1949)

Key point: Europeans pushed first

The slide emphasizes security institutions were European initiatives.

Europeans wanted:

  • U.S. guarantees
  • Protection from USSR
  • A solution to the “German problem”

Lundestad famously calls this dynamic “Empire by Invitation”, meaning Europeans invited U.S. leadership because their own security was impossible without it.

sections.title: XI. NATO and Article 5: The Break with Isolationism
sections.html:
The slide quotes Article 5: an attack on one is an attack on all.

Significance:

1. First U.S. peacetime alliance

This was unprecedented:

  • The U.S. had avoided permanent alliances since 1796
  • NATO marked the formal end of American isolationism

2. Collective defense against the USSR

  • Provided American nuclear umbrella
  • Institutionalized American leadership
  • Prevented Soviet intimidation of Western Europe

3. Sloan’s analysis

Sloan argues NATO embodied the transatlantic bargain:

  • U.S. = security guarantees and military presence
  • Europe = political alignment, bases, and acceptance of U.S. leadership

4. Not all members were democratic

The slide notes that early NATO included authoritarian regimes (e.g., Portugal).

This shows containment was guided by geopolitics, not ideals.

5. Institutions evolved later

Initially NATO was only a treaty; the permanent command structures (SHAPE, SACEUR) came in the early 1950s.

sections.title: XII. NSC-68 and the Globalization of Containment
sections.html:
The final slide highlights NSC-68, a decisive step in U.S. strategy (1950).- 66-page top secret US National Security Council (NSC) policy paper drafted by the Department of State and Department of Defense

Key elements:

  • U.S. must resist communism everywhere
  • Massive increases in military spending (hydrogen bomb)
  • Global Cold War (Korea began same year)
  • Europe as central front

This globalized the Truman Doctrine and finalized the abandonment of isolationism.

sections.title: XIII. Why 1945–1950 Marked the Permanent End of Isolationism
sections.html:
1. Europe invited the U.S. to stay (Lundestad)

Security needs + fear of Germany + fear of the USSR = Europeans asked for U.S. leadership.

2. U.S. believed European collapse would endanger global stability (Cox & Kennedy-Pipe) Economic reconstruction was necessary for political stability.

3. Truman’s worldview hardened (Offner)

Moral clarity + distrust of the USSR → willingness to lead.

4. Military institutionalization (Sloan)

NATO transformed temporary commitments into permanent obligations.

5. Cold War confrontation made disengagement impossible

By 1950, Europe was the frontline of a global ideological conflict.

sections.title: XIV. Conclusion: The Birth of the Transatlantic System
sections.html:
Between 1945 and 1950, the United States:

  • Rejected isolationism
  • Built a permanent military presence in Europe
  • Implemented containment
  • Launched the Marshall Plan
  • Encouraged European integration
  • Created NATO
  • Established the foundations of the Cold War international order

This period marks the true birth of modern transatlantic relations — a system held together by:

  • shared interests
  • shared institutions
  • shared threats
  • and a shared understanding that European security and American security were inseparable.

lectures.title: The United States and the German Problem

sections.title: I. Introduction: Why Germany Became the Central Problem of the Cold War
sections.html:
Germany’s division after World War II was not merely a geographic separation — it was the core strategic, ideological, and psychological battleground of the early Cold War. The PowerPoint stresses that Germany was “the central problem of postwar Europe,” and also “the central problem of the Cold War” itself.

This is because Germany was:

  • Europe’s economic and industrial heart
  • Strategic center of the continent
  • Divided into occupation zones by the victors
  • A potential prize for either the Soviet or Western sphere

As Bessel shows, in 1945 Germany was a ruined society, politically collapsed, physically destroyed, yet still strategically essential. It was a vacuum the Allies sought to fill with radically different visions.

France wanted security and limits on German power.

The USSR wanted a buffer and dominance.

The U.S. wanted stability and reconstruction.

Britain wanted balance and to prevent either hegemon.

Thus the division of Germany was structural, not accidental: the power configuration, ideological conflict, and incompatible security goals ensured the split.

The period 1945–1961 is the story of how temporary occupation zones hardened into two separate states, and how Berlin — deep inside the Soviet zone — became the Cold War’s “most dangerous place.”

sections.title: II. Germany 1945: Collapse, Occupation, and the Seeds of Division
sections.html:
1. Germany in ruins (Bessel)

Germany in 1945 was not simply defeated — it was shattered, socially, economically, and morally. Bessel’s first chapters highlight:

  • Cities destroyed (Hamburg, Dresden, Cologne)
  • Millions homeless and displaced
  • Transportation, industry, and fuel systems collapsed
  • Famine and malnutrition widespread
  • Social order disintegrated
  • The Nazi state gone, replaced by vacuum and chaos

The collapse created a space for external powers to reshape Germany.

2. Allied occupation planning: agreed on disarmament, not on Germany’s political future

Slides and readings show that the Allies agreed on:

  • Demilitarization
  • Denazification
  • Decartelization
  • Democratization

But they disagreed intensely on:

  • centralization vs. decentralization
  • economic policy (reconstruction vs. deindustrialization)
  • Germany as neutral, unified state OR divided buffer zones

France wanted Germany weak, decentralized, potentially partitioned.

The USSR wanted control over unified Germany OR a weak neutral Germany.

The U.S. initially had no clear plan, but gradually supported reconstruction.

These incompatible visions made unity unlikely.

sections.title: III. The German Problem After WWII: Why All Sides Feared Germany Differently
sections.html:
1. French fears of a revived threat (Creswell & Trachtenberg)

France’s priority, as Creswell/Trachtenberg demonstrate, was security through weakening Germany. They feared:

  • resurgence of German power
  • renewed aggression
  • the industrial strength of the Ruhr (coal/steel)
  • loss of control over continental balance

Thus France pushed for:

  • internationalization of the Ruhr
  • dismantling German heavy industry
  • possibly permanent partition of Germany

French policy was guided by the trauma of 1870, 1914, and 1940 — all German invasions across the Rhine. For France, Germany unified = existential danger.

2. Soviet fears and goals

For the USSR, Germany had twice been the invasion route to Moscow (1914, 1941). Stalin wanted:

  • a friendly, socialist Germany
  • reparations
  • political control over Eastern Europe
  • guarantees Germany would never again threaten the USSR

The Soviets initially hoped for a unified Germany under their influence.

But when it became clear the Western Allies would prevent this, the USSR began constructing the GDR.

3. U.S. concerns

The U.S. feared:

  • German collapse leading to communist expansion
  • a divided Europe
  • economic chaos feeding radicalism
  • Soviet dominance of a united Germany

American policy shifted from punitive (Morgenthau) to reconstruction:

  • Marshall Plan
  • rebuilding West German industry
  • shifting from demilitarization to rearmament

This reflects the Kennan strategy: Germany must be strong enough to resist communism but embedded in Western institutions.

sections.title: IV. From Occupation to Division: The Breakdown of Allied Cooperation
sections.html:
The PowerPoint stresses critical events turning occupation zones into political blocs.

1. Failure of the Allied Control Council

The Council required unanimity; disagreements made joint governance impossible.

Western economic integration (Bizonia → Trizonia) signaled the beginning of separation.

2. The Marshall Plan (1947)

The Marshall Plan was offered to all zones, including the Soviet zone.

Its rejection by Stalin hardened the divide.

Cox & Kennedy-Pipe note this was a geopolitical decision, cementing Western reconstruction vs. Eastern isolation.

3. Currency reform (1948)

The introduction of the Deutsche Mark in the Western zones was a major trigger:

  • Soviet fear of economic integration in the West
  • Response: blockade of West Berlin (1948–49)

4. The Berlin Blockade and Airlift

The slides highlight this as decisive.

  • Soviets blocked all land access
  • U.S. responded with the Airlift
  • Symbolized the West’s commitment to Berlin
  • Political victory for U.S. and humiliation for USSR

Kempe covers how Clay defied pessimistic estimates and proved the West would not abandon Berlin.

The Airlift shifted German public opinion strongly toward the West.

sections.title: V. Creation of Two German States (1949)
sections.html:
1. Federal Republic of Germany (FRG)

Established May 1949

  • Western zones unified
  • Parliamentary democracy
  • Konrad Adenauer becomes Chancellor
  • Integrated into Western economic and security structures

2. German Democratic Republic (GDR)

Established October 1949

  • Soviet-controlled zone
  • Socialist one-party state
  • Mass emigration weakens legitimacy

3. Why division became permanent

Slides emphasize factors such as:

  • incompatible political systems
  • Cold War intensification
  • NATO (1949) vs. Warsaw Pact (1955)
  • Economic divergence (Wirtschaftswunder vs. stagnation)

sections.title: VI. Berlin: The Most Dangerous Place in the Cold War
sections.html:
Berlin became the focal point of East–West tensions because:

  • It was located deep inside the GDR
  • It hosted Allied garrisons
  • It symbolized ideological competition
  • Its freedom undermined the legitimacy of the East German regime

1. West Berlin as showcase of capitalism

  • Economically tied to FRG
  • Symbol of Western freedom
  • Escape route for millions of East Germans

2. East German crisis: mass flight / brain drain

Between 1949–1961, over 2.5 million East Germans defected through Berlin.

Kempe emphasizes:

  • loss of skilled workers
  • ideological embarrassment
  • pressure on Ulbricht to stop the exodus

sections.title: VII. Eisenhower, Military Strategy, and the Berlin Pressure Points (Coleman)
sections.html:
Coleman's work clarifies U.S. military thinking in the 1950s:

1. Eisenhower’s strategy: avoid war but maintain resolve

  • Belief: weak signals encourage Soviet pressure
  • Berlin = test of U.S. credibility
  • Show firmness without provoking war

2. Nuclear deterrence

Eisenhower relied heavily on nuclear deterrence (“massive retaliation”).

Berlin crises were managed not by conventional buildup but by credible nuclear threat.

3. Preparing for contingencies

Coleman details contingency planning for:

  • Soviet blockade
  • harassment of Western convoys
  • potential withdrawal scenarios
  • keeping access routes open

Eisenhower believed Berlin must be held, but the U.S. must avoid being dragged into war on unfavorable terms.

sections.title: VIII. France and the German Question (Creswell & Trachtenberg)
sections.html:
Slides emphasize French influence in both the early division and later rearmament debates.

1. French strategy: weaken and control Germany

  • Internationalize Ruhr
  • Push for decentralization
  • Limit German sovereignty
  • Maintain occupation rights

2. French fear of U.S.–German rapprochement

France worried the U.S. might:

  • rebuild German power too fast
  • favor Germany over French security
  • tolerate centralization dangerous to France

3. Berlin as a French concern

Any shift in Berlin policy threatened French security calculus.

Thus French resistance shaped:

  • the pace of German sovereignty
  • NATO structure
  • the European Defense Community (EDC)

sections.title: IX. The Berlin Crisis of 1958–1961
sections.html:
Slides cover Khrushchev’s ultimatums:

  • West must negotiate Berlin status
  • Threat to sign peace treaty with GDR
  • Threat to end Allied access

1. Why Khrushchev acted (Kempe + slides)

  • GDR near collapse from emigration
  • Need to stabilize East Germany
  • Strengthen Soviet standing in communist world
  • Test inexperienced U.S. leadership (Eisenhower late, then Kennedy)

2. The U-2 affair (1960)

  • Shot-down U.S. spy plane wrecked summit diplomacy
  • Khrushchev used crisis to gain leverage

3. Kennedy’s challenges (1961)

Kempe’s narrative shows a hesitant, inconsistent Kennedy:

  • Initially unsure of Berlin strategy
  • Publicly tough (“Ich bin Berliner's future”)
  • Privately unsure whether to risk war
  • Keen to avoid escalation

Soviets interpreted his early caution as weakness.

sections.title: X. The Berlin Wall (August 13, 1961)
sections.html:
Slides: “Construction of the Wall” — central event.

1. Why the Wall was built

  • Stop mass emigration
  • Preserve GDR regime stability
  • Remove ideological embarrassment
  • Avoid collapse of East German economy

2. Why Soviets approved

  • Ulbricht pushed hard
  • Khrushchev saw Wall as lesser evil compared to losing the GDR
  • Avoided direct confrontation with U.S. while sealing the border

3. U.S. reaction

Kempe shows:

  • Kennedy was shocked but relieved — Wall was better than war
  • Clay returned to Berlin to reassure West Berliners
  • Showed presence and resolve (Steinstücken episode)

4. Checkpoint Charlie standoff (October 1961)

Tanks faced each other at short range.

Kempe details:

  • Clay pushed for strong response
  • Kennedy privately worried about escalation
  • Soviets eventually withdrew tanks first
  • Demonstrated how dangerous Berlin was

The Wall froze the division and symbolized the Cold War’s permanence.

sections.title: XI. The Consolidation of Division (Post-1961)
sections.html:
Slides hint at consequences:

  • East Germany firmly in Soviet bloc
  • West Germany firmly in NATO
  • Berlin no longer escape route
  • Cold War stabilized but hardened
  • Two Germanies institutionalized

The Wall did not solve the Cold War but removed the most immediate crisis of population flight.

sections.title: XII. Conclusion: Why Germany’s Division Defined the Cold War
sections.html:
Germany became the geopolitical core of the entire Cold War because:

1. It was economically central to Europe.

2. Its political alignment determined strategic balance.

3. It embodied ideological competition between communism and democracy.

4. Berlin symbolized the clash of freedoms vs. authoritarian control.

5. Both blocs feared a united Germany in the camp of the other.

6. Division solved immediate postwar dilemmas but created long-term confrontation.

By 1961, the division of Germany was irreversible — and it remained the defining geopolitical fault line until 1989–1990.

lectures.title: The US and the overseas European Empires, and the impact of the Cold War

sections.title: I. Introduction: Decolonisation as a Transatlantic Issue
sections.html:
The presentation begins with a series of questions that frame the entire lecture:

  • What were America’s traditional views on European empires?
  • How did WWII alter U.S. thinking on imperialism?
  • How much pressure did the U.S. put on Britain and France?
  • How significant was U.S. influence in ending European empires?
  • How did the Cold War reshape decolonisation?
  • Why did the U.S. and U.K. clash over Egypt in 1956?

To answer these, we must view decolonisation not just as a regional process but a global transformation in power, legitimacy, and economic structures — a central argument from Hopkins: decolonisation after 1945 was part of a broader shift in globalisation, where territorial empires no longer made sense economically or morally.

The U.S. becomes central not because it had a colonial policy — it claimed not to — but because it redefined international norms, pressured European allies, and viewed colonialism through strategic, ideological, and economic lenses.

sections.title: II. European Colonialism Before WWII
sections.html:
1. The Structure and Logic of Empire

The slide that simply states “European colonialism” introduces the baseline:

Europe’s global dominance was built on:

  • Military superiority
  • Economic extraction
  • Racial ideologies and paternalistic “civilising missions”
  • Control of trade routes and raw materials
  • Legal frameworks that subordinated colonised peoples

Hobsbawm emphasizes that in the 19th century Western states dominated the world not simply through armies, but through capitalism, industrialisation, and control of global markets. These states exported their institutions and economies, remaking the world system around their needs.

This model seemed stable — until WWII.

sections.title: III. European Decolonisation: Why It Happened
sections.html:
1. Material Causes

The slides list “Material reasons for decolonisation,” which align with major scholarly arguments:

a. Exhaustion from WWII

  • Britain and France emerged economically devastated.
  • Their balance sheets could no longer support vast colonial bureaucracies and militaries.
  • Hopkins notes the “material conditions that underpinned territorial empires dissolved” after the war.

b. Rising cost of holding empire

  • Counter-insurgency wars (Malaya, Kenya, Indochina, Algeria) were expensive.
  • Taxpayers in Europe increasingly questioned why they were paying for distant conflicts.

c. Changing global economy

  • Globalisation shifted: economic integration no longer required territorial control.
  • Trade and finance became more important than rule.

This shift made the empire economically irrational.

2. Non-Material Causes

The slide also distinguishes non-material factors, emphasizing changing global norms:

a. Rise of nationalism

Colonised peoples increasingly demanded sovereignty. Hobsbawm stresses that anti-colonial movements were inspired by:

  • Western education
  • Ideas of self-determination
  • Socialism and anti-imperial ideologies
  • Religious revivalism in some cases

b. Global legitimacy crisis

Hopkins argues that the moral order supporting empire collapsed:

  • Human rights became a new international norm.
  • Colonial rule became seen as incompatible with post-war ideals.
  • The UN system delegitimised empire and elevated anti-colonial claims.

c. Perception of empire after Nazi occupation

Europeans experienced occupation and oppression. This undermined the moral basis of imperial domination — especially in France and the Netherlands.

sections.title: IV. The U.S. and European Imperialism Before WWII
sections.html:
1. A Contradictory American Tradition

The lecture slide shows Franklin Roosevelt’s famous quote:

“He’s a SOB, but he’s our SOB.” (referring to Trujillo)

This illustrates U.S. hypocrisy:

  • Officially anti-colonial (rooted in its own revolutionary history)
  • Practically imperial in Latin America and the Philippines

(Louis notes that U.S. anti-colonialism historically coexisted with strategic self-interest and willingness to prop up local dictators when beneficial.)

Hopkins also argues the U.S. itself underwent an internal and external form of “decolonisation,” as its territories (Philippines, Puerto Rico, Hawaii) transitioned away from colonial rule post-1945 — often under pressure similar to European empires.

sections.title: V. U.S. Anti-Imperialism and the British Empire
sections.html:
1. American suspicion of the British Empire

From the 19th century to WWII, American elites often saw the British Empire as:

  • anti-democratic
  • economically restrictive
  • an obstacle to free trade (an important point stressed by Louis)

Life Magazine in 1942 reflects popular sentiment:

“One thing we are not fighting for is to hold the British Empire together…”

This shows American frustration with what appeared to be British hypocrisy: fighting fascism while denying Indians and Africans self-government.

2. Churchill vs. Roosevelt

Churchill’s quote:

“I did not become the King’s First Minister to preside over the liquidation of the British Empire.”

This captures the huge clash:

  • Churchill equated empire with Britain’s great-power status.
  • Roosevelt saw empire as outdated, immoral, and economically restrictive.

But Roosevelt’s policies were not purely idealistic.

LaFeber shows that he also wanted:

  • to weaken British influence
  • to expand American markets
  • to prevent European empires from dominating Asia again

Indochina became the most dramatic example.

sections.title: VI. Decolonisation of the British Empire
sections.html:
1. India as the turning point

Two slides highlight Indian independence.

Reasons:

  • The 1942 Quit India movement revealed mass nationalist mobilisation.
  • Post-war austerity made Britain unable to afford another long conflict.
  • The British feared mass civil war and mutiny.
  • U.S. pressure pushed for self-determination.

Louis stresses that American influence mattered:

  • U.S. criticism of British repression weakened legitimacy.
  • Washington saw Indian independence as stabilising Asia and reducing Soviet appeal.

2. Britain’s wider imperial retreat

Once India was gone, the entire imperial logic collapsed:

  • The empire’s economic “keystone” disappeared.
  • The Sterling Area weakened.
  • Britain shifted to a new strategy: managing decolonisation to preserve influence.

This is what Lundestad describes as “empire by integration” — the U.K. attempted to move from imperial control to partnerships through the Commonwealth and Europe.

sections.title: VII. The Cold War and Decolonisation
sections.html:
1. U.S. Priorities Change (Idealism → Containment)

After 1947, the U.S. increasingly prioritised fighting communism over fighting colonialism.

This produced contradictions:

  • America pressured the Dutch in Indonesia (idealistic phase, 1945–49)
  • But supported France in Indochina (containment phase)

Hopkins argues the Cold War imposed new priorities that often froze or distorted decolonisation, as both superpowers sought influence over new states.

2. Britain, the U.S., and the Middle East

Slides jump to Suez — the ultimate example of Cold War + decolonisation tension.

sections.title: VIII. Decolonisation of the French Empire
sections.html:
1. Indochina

This section must integrate LaFeber’s extensive material.

Roosevelt’s position during WWII:

  • Believed France was unfit to return to Indochina.
  • Proposed an international trusteeship.
  • Considered giving China a major role in post-war Asia.

FDR:

  • opposed French re-entry
  • feared resurgent European colonialism
  • saw Indochina as strategically vital

But:

  • Churchill opposed U.S. interference because he feared precedent for British colonies.
  • Chiang Kai-shek refused to support the trusteeship plan because he had no interest in governing Indochina.
  • State Department elites preferred restoring France to strengthen post-war Europe.

By 1945, Roosevelt abandoned the trusteeship idea.

This decision shaped:

  • the First Indochina War (1946–54)
  • French/American reliance on military force
  • the rise of Ho Chi Minh’s nationalist-communist coalition

2. Algeria

France’s war in Algeria symbolised:

  • the refusal to accept imperial decline
  • massive violence against civilians
  • the risk of military revolt in metropolitan France

U.S. attitudes were ambivalent:

  • Eisenhower and Dulles valued France as a NATO ally
  • They feared Algeria turning communist
  • But they discouraged French excesses and pushed for a negotiated solution Hopkins and Hobsbawm both underline that Algeria showed how colonial wars became politically unsustainablebecause global opinion rejected them.

sections.title: IX. The Suez Crisis (1956)
sections.html:
This is the climax of the lecture.

1. Causes

  • Egypt nationalised the Suez Canal (Nasser, 1956)
  • Britain and France saw this as a challenge to their prestige and economic interests
  • Israel joined the plot, hoping to weaken Egypt militarily

2. Anglo–American Clash

The slides highlight “Anglo-American tensions.”

This is the most important transatlantic rupture of the post-war era.

Why the U.S. opposed the invasion:

  • Eisenhower feared pushing Arab states toward the USSR
  • The U.S. opposed old-style imperialism — it violated post-war norms
  • Eisenhower was furious Britain and France had deceived Washington
  • The U.S. wanted stability in the Middle East under its influence, not Britain's Louis emphasises that Suez marked the end of the British Empire as a global power and demonstrated the growing asymmetry in Anglo-American relations.

3. Global consequences

  • The U.N. (with U.S. support) forced a ceasefire.
  • Britain suffered a financial crisis after the U.S. refused to support the pound.
  • Nasser became a hero of anti-colonial nationalism.
  • The USSR exploited Western humiliation for propaganda.
  • European decolonisation accelerated dramatically.

Lundestad describes Suez as the moment Britain realised it must pursue “integration” with Europe and the U.S. rather than imperial power projection.

sections.title: X. Out-of-Area Problems as a Defining Feature of Transatlantic Relations
sections.html:
What are “out-of-area” problems?

Issues outside the formal North Atlantic region but critical for:

  • global security
  • Cold War strategy
  • superpower competition
  • access to resources (oil, raw materials)
  • political legitimacy (anti-colonialism, human rights)

Examples:

  • Middle East (Suez, Iran, Iraq)
  • Asia (Indochina, Korea)
  • Africa (Congo, Kenya, Rhodesia)

Why America and Europe disagreed

Europe:

  • Sought to maintain influence in former colonies
  • Depended economically on access to imperial trade
  • Feared instability in newly independent regions

U.S.:

  • Anti-colonial in rhetoric
  • Pro-stability in practice
  • Saw nationalism as potential communist leverage
  • Wanted access to resources without colonial structures
  • Opposed old empires but supported neo-colonial arrangements

This produced a pattern:

  • U.S. pressure + Cold War + colonial weakness → forced decolonisation
  • But also new dependencies (aid, security cooperation, economic influence)

Hopkins underscores that this constituted a new form of post-colonial globalisation, where informal control replaced formal empire.

sections.title: XI. Conclusion: The Transatlantic Shift from Empire to Global Governance
sections.html:
By the late 1950s:

  • Britain & France had lost most of their empires.
  • The U.S. had emerged as the primary Western power in Africa, Asia, and the Middle East.
  • NATO increasingly faced “out-of-area” dilemmas: should the alliance intervene outside Europe? how should Western powers coordinate?
  • Decolonisation reshaped not only international relations but the Atlantic Alliance itself.

Lundestad summarises this transformation as the shift from empire to partnership, where the U.S. replaced European empires as the dominant Western actor — not through colonialism but through military alliances, economic integration, and political leadership.

lectures.title: Empire by Integration? The US and the European Project

sections.title: I. Introduction: Why European Integration Became a U.S. Strategic Priority
sections.html:
The central question from the presentation is:

Why and in what ways did the United States promote European integration in the postwar years?

This question is historically significant because the United States is the first great power in world history that:

  • encouraged the political and economic unification of other states,
  • helped build institutions above the nation-state level,
  • and willingly accepted regional blocs that might otherwise have become rivals.

This is exactly what Lundestad emphasises in Empire by Integration:

European integration was not an anti-American phenomenon — it was something that the U.S. actively promoted, because it served deep American strategic interests.

Thus, the U.S. is not an “empire” in the classic sense, but it exercised imperial influence through:

  • aid programs,
  • political pressure,
  • security guarantees,
  • and economic power, creating what Lundestad calls an “empire by integration.”

The lecture explores how this strategy developed between 1945 and the late 1960s.

sections.title: II. Background: Roots of the Idea of Europe Before U.S. Involvement
sections.html:
The presentation starts by reminding us that the idea of a united Europe is older than post-1945 integration:

  • Interwar movements promoted European unity (Pan-Europa, Briand plan).
  • Even Hitler had his own twisted vision of a unified, dominated Europe.
  • Churchill in 1946 famously called for a “United States of Europe.”

But none of these initiatives had the political, economic, or security conditions necessary to succeed.

WWII fundamentally changed everything:

  • Europe was physically destroyed and politically discredited.
  • Traditional great powers (Britain, France) were exhausted.
  • Germany was defeated and needed reintegration.
  • The Soviet Union posed a new threat.
  • The U.S. emerged as the indispensable Western power.

Thus, when the integration process began after 1945, it did so in a world where the United States had overwhelming influence — and where European countries were ready to accept that influence.

sections.title: III. U.S. Economic Thinking: Why America Needed a Strong Europe
sections.html:
The presentation quotes a U.S. economic administrator:

“We need a productive, thriving Europe as a market for our goods… the foreign purchaser won’t have money unless he, too, is producing and selling.”

This statement reflects core American thinking in 1945–48:

1. Economic interdependence → U.S. prosperity

The U.S. believed that European reconstruction was essential for:

  • exporting American industrial output,
  • preventing another Depression-like collapse,
  • keeping global capitalism functioning.

2. Europe must be rebuilt as an integrated unit

Lundestad notes that U.S. officials believed fragmented European economies:

  • were inefficient and unproductive,
  • relied too heavily on protectionism,
  • could not absorb American exports,
  • and would remain vulnerable to political instability.

3. Integration = economic rationalisation

Integration meant:

  • harmonising markets,
  • removing trade barriers,
  • achieving economies of scale,
  • making Germany’s economic revival politically acceptable.

A more united Europe would be economically useful to American global plans.

sections.title: IV. The Marshall Plan and Its Integrative Logic
sections.html:
The presentation includes a key Marshall statement:

“Our policy is not directed against any country… but against hunger, poverty, desperation and chaos.”

Yet the underlying logic was deeply strategic:

1. Marshall Aid forced Europeans to cooperate

The OEEC (Organisation for European Economic Cooperation) was created because:

  • the U.S. required collective administration of aid,
  • this compelled Europeans to plan together and share economic data,
  • integration began as a condition of receiving aid.

Lundestad emphasises that the U.S. used Marshall Aid as an instrument to:

  • push Europe toward multilateralism,
  • reduce barriers,
  • coordinate reconstruction.

2. The Plan became part of containment

The slide states explicitly:

“The Marshall Plan became an integral part of containment.”

Why?

  • A prosperous Western Europe would resist communism.
  • The U.S. believed economic collapse had aided fascism in the 1930s.
  • Aid was also a tool to keep Italy and France from drifting left.

3. Marshall Plan and European unity

The presentation notes that the Plan encouraged the beginnings of European unity.

Specifically, it:

  • revitalised the European movement,
  • strengthened pro-integration elites (Monnet, Schuman),
  • aligned national recovery plans.

Economic growth data (GDP % in slide) symbolises how U.S. aid triggered the Western “economic miracle.”

sections.title: V. Why the U.S. Wanted European Integration (Slide Breakdown)
sections.html:
The presentation provides a list; Lundestad provides the analytical foundation.

Here is the integrated explanation:

1. A “federal Europe” looked like the American model

Americans saw European unity as:

  • natural,
  • rational,
  • familiar.

Lundestad shows that many U.S. policymakers openly hoped Europe would adopt federal structures similar to the U.S. model.

2. A stronger, more efficient Europe helped global capitalism

  • Economic fragmentation created protectionism.
  • Larger markets → greater productivity → stable democracy.
  • The U.S. wanted a prosperous partner in global trade.

3. Europe could reduce the American burden

The U.S. did not want to permanently bankroll Europe.

Lundestad notes repeated American complaints from Truman to Johnson that Europeans were not “doing enough” — whether in NATO or economic policy.

4. Integration strengthened containment of the USSR

A politically united and economically strong Europe was:

  • a strategic buffer,
  • a partner in Cold War institutions,
  • a stabiliser preventing Soviet influence.

Integration therefore strengthened the Western bloc.

5. Integration solved the “German Problem”

This is the decisive motive.

  • Germany needed to be strong but controlled.
  • Integration tied Germany structurally to Western Europe.
  • France accepted German recovery because supranational institutions diluted German power.

Lundestad repeatedly stresses that U.S. policymakers viewed integration as the best possible solution to reintegrating Germany without allowing it to become a threat.

sections.title: VI. Britain and European Integration (Slide Analysis)
sections.html:
The presentation shows the famous British diplomat’s comment on the Messina negotiations:

“The future treaty has no chance of being agreed, or ratified, or applied — and if applied, would be unacceptable to Britain.”

This captures Britain’s early scepticism.

1. Britain “won the war” and still had a global empire

  • Britain believed it did not need supranational constraints.
  • It saw itself as a global, not merely European, power.

2. Churchill supported European unity… for others

As the slide notes:

  • Churchill supported integration in principle.
  • But he saw Britain as outside this project.
  • He preferred the Council of Europe, not the supranational ECSC.

3. Britain refused to join the early institutions

  • Rejected the Coal and Steel Community (1952).
  • Created EFTA (1960) as an intergovernmental alternative to the EEC.

4. U.S. reaction

Lundestad shows the U.S.:

  • Wanted Britain in the EEC as a balance to France and West Germany.
  • Saw British membership as strengthening Atlantic unity.

Thus, when De Gaulle vetoed Britain in 1963 and 1967, U.S. policymakers were deeply frustrated.

sections.title: VII. The First Steps Toward Integration (Slide + Lundestad Ch. 4)
sections.html:
1. Benelux Customs Union (1948)

This small-scale integration demonstrated successful cross-border cooperation.

2. The ECSC (1952)

The slide emphasises that coal and steel were “essential war materials.”

Monnet and Schuman understood that:

  • war would be materially impossible if these sectors were supranational,
  • France and Germany would be mutually dependent.

Lundestad notes the U.S.:

  • strongly endorsed the ECSC,
  • saw it as the first real breakthrough.

3. EDC failure (1954)

The presentation mentions the collapse of the European Defence Community.

Lundestad explains that:

  • the U.S. strongly supported EDC,
  • Dulles threatened consequences if it failed,
  • France itself rejected the treaty.

This failure pushed Europe toward NATO-based defence and away from military integration.

sections.title: VIII. Treaty of Rome (1957): Foundation of the EEC
sections.html:
The slide shows the birth of:

  • EEC
  • EURATOM

1. Britain again excluded itself

It preferred EFTA (an intergovernmental approach) to the supranational logic of the EEC.

2. The U.S. response

Lundestad reports that:

  • the U.S. accepted the EEC despite its trade discrimination,
  • because political unity outweighed short-term economic costs,
  • but hoped the GATT would reduce tariff discrimination overall.

Integration was acceptable as long as it stayed aligned with U.S. strategic goals through NATO and Atlantic institutions.

sections.title: IX. The Atlantic Framework (Lundestad Ch. 5)
sections.html:
The slide explicitly refers to this.

Lundestad writes that the U.S.:

  • insisted integration must be nested inside the Atlantic order,
  • saw NATO as the overarching structure,
  • opposed any independent European pole,
  • wanted cooperation, not competition.

Thus:

U.S. policy = integrate Europe BUT prevent Europe from becoming a rival power centre.

This explains American attitudes toward:

  • British bids for membership,
  • De Gaulle’s challenge,
  • NATO leadership,
  • economic institutions.

sections.title: X. De Gaulle’s Challenge (Slide + Lundestad Ch. 6)
sections.html:
De Gaulle’s actions directly threatened the U.S. vision:

1. He vetoed British membership (1963, 1967)

  • He believed Britain would be a “Trojan horse” for U.S. influence.
  • U.S. policymakers were extremely frustrated.

2. He withdrew French forces from NATO’s integrated command (1966)

Although France remained in NATO politically, this weakened the alliance’s military structure.

3. He promoted a “Europe of Nations”

Opposing:

  • supranationalism,
  • strong Commission authority,
  • federalist tendencies.

4. U.S. response: calm, supportive of integration

Lundestad shows that:

  • the U.S. refused to confront De Gaulle head-on,
  • but quietly strengthened ties with Germany and the Commission,
  • upheld the idea of a supranational Europe.

sections.title: XI. Johnson and European Integration (Guderzo)
sections.html:
The presentation includes late-1960s evolution; Guderzo provides detail for this period.

Guderzo challenges older views that Johnson neglected Europe:

1. Johnson did care about Europe

He spent “a substantial part of my time dealing with Europeans,” according to the Johnson quote on slide.

Guderzo confirms this (p. 100).

2. Core U.S. concerns under LBJ

  • European complaints about neglect
  • Burden-sharing in NATO
  • British economic weakness
  • Tensions with De Gaulle
  • Ongoing trade negotiations (Kennedy Round)

3. “Cautious optimism” (1967)

Guderzo notes (p. 94–95):

  • Germany stable and strong
  • France recovering from crisis
  • Wilson’s UK government prepared to enter the EEC
  • Atlantic relations seemed more promising

4. Continuous U.S. support — but conditional

Johnson supported integration as long as:

  • It stayed Atlantic-oriented
  • It did not conflict with U.S. interests
  • It strengthened Western cohesion

sections.title: XII. Conclusion: The U.S. as Architect and Constraint of European Integration
sections.html:
Across all files, several core themes emerge:

1. The U.S. was the most important external force behind European integration

The presentation and Lundestad agree fully.

2. U.S. motives were strategic, economic, and ideological

Integration helped:

  • containment,
  • reconstruction,
  • management of Germany,
  • the Atlantic system.

3. Integration had limits

U.S. support depended on Europe:

  • remaining within NATO,
  • avoiding an independent bloc,
  • adding to — not subtracting from — American leadership.

4. De Gaulle was the biggest challenge

Yet U.S. support continued despite him.

5. LBJ did not abandon integration

Guderzo’s article clarifies this underappreciated point.

6. Europe’s integration both depended on and rebalanced the Atlantic partnership

The U.S. encouraged integration — but not at the expense of the Atlantic framework.

lectures.title: Troublesome Allies (1): the US and de Gaulle

sections.title: 1. Introduction: Why the US–France Relationship Became “Troublesome”
sections.html:
The Cold War began in Europe and rapidly expanded into a global confrontation. Although Europe after 1953 was relatively stable—frozen into two opposing “empires” (NATO and the Soviet bloc)—the United States’ leadership position weakened by the 1960s.

  • Early 1950s: Europeans depended heavily on Washington.
  • By the 1960s: Economic recovery, colonial crises, nuclear proliferation, and growing US commitments in Vietnam made European allies more assertive and less deferential.

The most visible challenge to American leadership came from Charles de Gaulle, whose ambition was to restore France as an autonomous global power and reduce US (and British) dominance in Europe.

sections.title: 2. American Allies in the 1950s–60s: Mixed Support and Emerging Friction
sections.html:
2.1 Early Cooperation

  • Paris Accords (1955): West Germany rearmament & NATO membership—Europe unified behind US leadership.
  • But 1956 Suez Crisis completely reshaped dynamics:
  • Britain and France invaded Egypt without US approval.
  • The United States forced them to withdraw, demonstrating American supremacy.

2.2 Post-Suez Divergence

  • France: humiliated; concluded US power was too dominant → began distancing itself.
  • Britain: despite Suez, doubled down on the special relationship to retain influence.
  • Both Britain and France developed nuclear weapons to assert autonomy.

2.3 Burden-Sharing Becomes a Flashpoint

By the early 1960s, the US complained that Europeans depended militarily on the American nuclear umbrella while:

  • contributing less financially and militarily,
  • criticizing American policy decisions.

President Eisenhower expressed this frustration:

Europeans took US money, resisted US advice, and then criticized the United States loudly.

sections.title: 3. Nuclear Weapons and Transatlantic Tensions
sections.html:
3.1 Nuclear Proliferation in Western Europe

  • Britain developed its bomb in 1953.
  • The US revived nuclear cooperation with the UK in 1958.
  • France tested its first bomb in 1960, creating an independent force de frappe.
  • The US proposed a Multilateral Nuclear Force (MLF) to give Germany a controlled nuclear role.
  • But the project failed — especially because de Gaulle opposed it.

3.2 Why de Gaulle Opposed the MLF

De Gaulle saw the MLF as:

  • a US attempt to keep control of Europe,
  • a tool to prevent France from becoming Europe’s leading nuclear power,
  • a mechanism that could empower West Germany in dangerous ways.

He believed true European independence required:

  • national nuclear forces (hence the French bomb),
  • ending dependence on the American deterrent.

The readings confirm that de Gaulle viewed supranational nuclear arrangements as a threat to sovereignty (e.g., from NATO crisis analyses in Wenger’s Crisis and Opportunity ).

sections.title: 4. Charles de Gaulle: Vision, Grievances, and Goals
sections.html:
4.1 De Gaulle’s Core Worldview

He believed:

  • France remained a global nation that had lost its rightful leadership role.
  • The United States and the United Kingdom formed an “Anglo-Saxon bloc” marginalizing France.
  • Europe should be led by continental powers, not the US or UK.

His famous ambition was a “Europe from the Atlantic to the Urals” — a geopolitical space independent of superpower dominance.

4.2 Experiences in WWII Fueled Distrust

De Gaulle’s difficult wartime relationship with Roosevelt convinced him that the United States:

  • had tried to sideline France,
  • preferred dealing with Britain,
  • would always seek preeminence.

This created a lasting suspicion of American motives.

sections.title: 5. De Gaulle’s Step-by-Step Challenge to NATO
sections.html:
The presentation lays out France’s gradual detachment:

5.1 Partial Withdrawals (1959–1964)

  • 1959: withdrew Mediterranean fleet from NATO command.
  • 1963: withdrew Atlantic fleet.
