  • 1964: refused to sign the Test Ban Treaty, keeping nuclear independence.

5.2 Full Break with Integrated Command (1966)

In March 1966, de Gaulle formally removed France from NATO’s integrated military command, demanding:

  • all NATO troops leave French territory by 1967,
  • full sovereignty over French military decisions,
  • that NATO headquarters relocate (ultimately to Brussels).

This was a seismic shock: the first major structural crisis in NATO since 1949, described extensively in the scholarship (e.g., NATO crisis reconstructions in Wenger’s article ).

5.3 Key Motivations Behind the Withdrawal

  • Nuclear sovereignty: no reliance on US strategic decisions.
  • Geopolitical autonomy: France as a mediator between East and West.
  • Containment of Germany: stop FRG from gaining nuclear leverage through US-controlled arrangements.
  • Anti-hegemony: refusal to accept US dominance in NATO structures.

sections.title: 6. Reconfiguring NATO in Response
sections.html:
The US and remaining allies responded pragmatically rather than confrontationally.

6.1 US Internal Debate

Documents in the Wenger reading show:

  • Some US officials wanted to confront France publicly.
  • But Johnson chose a quiet, patient approach:
  • Preserve NATO unity among the remaining 14.
  • Avoid giving de Gaulle a propaganda victory.

6.2 Institutional Reforms

NATO restructured itself:

  • Defense Planning Committee (DPC) became the key military decision body (France absent).
  • New NATO headquarters established in Brussels.
  • Nuclear Planning Group (NPG) formed to allow other Europeans (especially West Germany) a role in nuclear discussion without proliferation (as detailed in Wenger’s analysis of the Harmel process ).

6.3 Expansion of NATO’s Political Role

De Gaulle claimed détente made NATO obsolete.

The others responded by expanding NATO’s political function—through the Harmel Report (1967):

  • NATO must combine deterrence + détente.
  • Alliances must consult on East–West diplomacy, not only military policy.

This directly countered de Gaulle’s argument that détente should bypass NATO.

sections.title: 7. De Gaulle’s Foreign Policy Goals: A Multi-Directional Strategy
sections.html:
7.1 Restoring French Grandeur

The force de frappe gave France symbolic equality with superpowers.

7.2 Reducing “Anglo-Saxon” Influence

De Gaulle:

  • vetoed British EEC entry twice (1963, 1967),
  • treated British nuclear ties to the US as incompatible with European independence,
  • viewed the UK as a US “Trojan horse”.

7.3 Opening to Eastern Europe & the USSR

As documented in Upsetting the Applecart (Jackson, Ch. 26) :

  • De Gaulle pursued early détente with Moscow (1966 visit).
  • Saw Eastern Europe’s industrial modernization as a chance to weaken bipolarity.

7.4 Containing Germany

De Gaulle feared:

  • German nationalism,
  • German nuclear ambitions,
  • a repeat of the 20th-century pattern of German centrality.

Thus, France’s détente with the USSR also had a strong anti-German dimension.

sections.title: 8. France and the United States on Global Issues
sections.html:
8.1 The Vietnam War

De Gaulle denounced the US war in Vietnam:

  • condemned it as colonial-style intervention (Phnom Penh speech, 1966),
  • attempted to position France as a mediator,
  • argued the US was preventing global détente.

The US saw this as hypocrisy, given France’s colonial record.

8.2 The Middle East Crisis (1967)

De Gaulle:

  • warned Israel “do not attack”, viewing it as expansionist (Eban meeting detailed in Jackson’s chapter ),
  • imposed an arms embargo once war began,
  • made his famous remark about “the Jewish people, sure of themselves and domineering”, which caused diplomatic uproar.

This episode deepened US–French estrangement.

8.3 Decolonization

France’s messy Algerian War contrasted with:

  • US rhetoric of anti-colonialism,
  • but also US support for certain right-wing dictators (as discussed in previous study guides).

De Gaulle positioned France as a post-colonial actor able to speak to the developing world.

sections.title: 9. Endgame: The End of de Gaulle and Shifting Transatlantic Relations
sections.html:
9.1 May 1968 Crisis

Mass protests undermined de Gaulle’s authority.

9.2 Failed Referendum (1969)

His proposed constitutional reform was defeated; he resigned.

9.3 Aftermath

Successors:

  • brought France closer to NATO,
  • softened anti-American rhetoric,
  • accepted multilateral European integration more readily.

Thus, the peak of transatlantic tension ended with de Gaulle’s departure.

sections.title: 10. Conclusion: Why the US–France Relationship Was “Troublesome”
sections.html:
France’s challenge was unique because:

  • it came from within the Western bloc,
  • it questioned both US leadership and NATO’s structure,
  • it combined nationalism, nuclear independence, and geopolitical ambition.

The United States responded by:

  • reforming NATO,
  • strengthening consultation,
  • accepting more political multilateralism,
  • avoiding direct confrontation.

The crisis ultimately strengthened NATO by forcing institutional adaptation and defining NATO as both a military and political alliance.

L1S1: Which three competing intellectual traditions of U.S. foreign policy does Lecture 1 introduce?
The lecture frames U.S. policy as a struggle between Realism and Idealism, with Liberalism as a hybrid.
How did America see itself relative to Europe culturally vs. geographically?
Part of Europe culturally, separate from it geographically and strategically
Separate culturally, but part of Europe strategically
A European colony even after independence
This dual identity is captured by the phrase 'America – off-shore Europe'.
L1S2: What phrase captures America's dual identity toward Europe?
America saw itself as a European offshoot but physically separate, able to stay detached from Europe's power struggles.
American policy toward Europe historically oscillated between which two poles?
Distance let the U.S. alternate between shaping order and avoiding entanglements.
Which European political tradition did the U.S. especially inherit?
The U.S. inherited European institutions, especially British liberal traditions, yet believed distance let it avoid Europe's corruption and wars.
L1S3: Which tradition sees America as a 'city upon a hill' with a moral mission to lead by example?
Idealism draws on the Puritan mission, Jeffersonian universalism and Wilson's Fourteen Points.
Which tradition views Europe mainly as a zone where a hostile hegemon could upset the global balance of power?
Realism stresses national interest, security, balance of power and engagement only when vital interests are at stake (Napoleon, Kaiser, Hitler, Stalin).
Liberalism is best described in the lecture as a blend of:
Liberalism supports rules-based cooperation, free trade and institutions like the League, UN and NATO; it's the intellectual backbone of the post-1945 order.
Which is NOT listed as a source of the Idealist tradition?
Mahanian sea power is a strategic (realist) idea linked to 1898, not to Idealism.
L1S4: What did Washington's Farewell Address warn against?
Permanent alliances with any portion of the foreign world
All foreign trade
Diplomatic relations with Britain
Westward expansion
It was a warning against entangling military and political commitments in Europe, not against trade or diplomacy.
Which was a reason Washington gave this advice?
The young U.S. was weak and could be entrapped in Europe's great-power rivalries
The U.S. was already the strongest power
Congress had banned foreign trade
France had declared war on the U.S.
The U.S. was weak, distant, and wanted to avoid Europe's 'ambition, rivalship, humor, or caprice'.
For roughly how long did Washington's doctrine guide U.S. foreign policy?
Over a century
About ten years
Only until the War of 1812
It was never followed
It remained the guiding doctrine for over a century; NATO (1949) formally ended it.
L1S5: Whose charts on manufacturing output and national income does the lecture use?
Paul Kennedy's data show the material foundations of U.S. power changing from 1750 to 1914.
According to Kennedy's data, by 1914 U.S. GNP:
By 1914 U.S. manufacturing surpassed every European country and its GNP exceeded Germany + Britain combined.
Where did the U.S. navy rank by 1914?
U.S. naval power rose dramatically to 3rd largest by 1914.
L1S6: Why is the Spanish-American War (1898) called a watershed?
It was America's first major overseas intervention and broke with strict isolationism
It was the first war the U.S. lost
It marks the beginning of America's 'Rise to Globalism'.
Which territories did the U.S. take from Spain?
Hawaii was annexed separately in the same period, but the former Spanish colonies were the Philippines, Guam and Puerto Rico.
What event in Havana Harbor in February 1898 ignited public outrage?
The explosion and sinking of the USS Maine
The USS Maine exploded, killing 268 sailors; the exact cause is still debated.
Which strategic doctrine drove the search for naval bases in 1898?
Strategic interests in naval bases followed Mahanian sea power ideas.
L1S7: Which factors drew the U.S. into WWI in 1917?
Unrestricted submarine warfare and the Zimmermann Telegram
Pearl Harbor and the Atlantic Charter
The Berlin Blockade
The Suez Crisis
Plus economic ties to Britain and France and Wilson's aim to make the world 'safe for democracy'.
What happened to Wilson's League of Nations in the U.S.?
The Senate rejected it, marking a return to isolationism
Congress made it a NATO precursor
The U.S. joined and led it
It was replaced by the Marshall Plan
Fear of entanglements and of losing Congress's war power drove the rejection.
What was a consequence of the U.S. rejecting the League?
Lack of U.S. engagement contributed to interwar instability
Immediate creation of the UN
A permanent U.S. army in Europe
German disarmament succeeded
Europe rebuilt an unstable order; depression and fascism grew unchecked — a lesson that shaped post-1945 policy.
L1S8: Which legislation did the U.S. pass in the interwar period to avoid war?
The Neutrality Acts
The Vandenberg Resolution
Lend-Lease
NSC-68
Neutrality Acts, rejection of the League and focus on the New Deal defined American retreat.
What did the U.S. underestimate in the interwar period ('strategic blindness')?
How isolationism can enable aggression
The power of the British Empire
The cost of the Marshall Plan
The danger of Soviet nuclear weapons
It also underestimated how economic collapse destabilises politics and how authoritarian regimes exploit power vacuums.
Which of these did post-1945 U.S. strategy embrace as a lesson of the interwar failure?
Permanent alliances (NATO)
Neutrality Acts
Rejection of collective security
Withdrawal from Europe
The lessons led to institutions, collective security, European reconstruction and permanent alliances.
L1S9: Which tradition best explains the Marshall Plan and support for the UN, IMF and World Bank?
Liberalism explains economic interdependence as a peace strategy.
Which tradition best explains containment of the USSR and NATO?
Realism explains balance-of-power logic, intervention in two world wars and military alliances.
Which tradition best explains Wilsonian rhetoric and belief in exceptionalism?
Idealism explains support for democracy, human rights and moral framing.
Together, the three traditions explain why the U.S. is:
They also explain why Europe is both a partner and an object of U.S. strategy.
L1S10: What does the conclusion of Lecture 1 argue about the transatlantic relationship?
It has deep roots and is not merely a post-1945 creation
It began only with NATO in 1949
It was invented by de Gaulle
It rests on shared origins, cycles of isolation and engagement, industrial power shifts and competing traditions.
L2S1: How did the U.S. emerge from WWII according to Lecture 2?
As a junior partner of Britain
It had unprecedented capabilities, a global network of military positions, ideological confidence and a strategic vision for Europe.
Which three readings are cited for Lecture 2?
These provide deeper insight into why the U.S. acted as it did after the war.
L2S2: What did FDR say in his Fireside Chat of 3 September 1939?
He could not ask Americans to remain neutral in thought as well
America would declare war on Germany immediately
The U.S. would never help Britain
Pearl Harbor was a day of infamy
He reframed neutrality as compatible with sympathy for victims of aggression, preparing opinion for Lend-Lease.
Churchill's June 1940 speech said Britain would fight until when?
Until the New World steps forth to rescue the Old
Until France surrendered
Until the League of Nations intervened
Until the Soviet Union joined
Churchill framed the U.S. role as historically destined.
Which was NOT a reason the U.S. stayed out of the war in 1939?
The Atlantic Charter forbade entry
The Neutrality Acts
Post-WWI hostility to entanglements
The Great Depression
The Atlantic Charter came later (August 1941) and defined shared war aims.
L2S3: Which of these was a principle of the Atlantic Charter (August 1941)?
It also included no territorial aggrandisement, free trade and collective security — foreshadowing the liberal order.
It was a joint Anglo-American declaration of war aims.
Why did Pearl Harbor (7 Dec 1941) change everything?
It united opinion, ended isolationist politics and launched the U.S. as a global power
It caused the Senate to reject the League
It led to the U.S. leaving the war
Germany then declared war on the U.S. in solidarity with Japan.
U.S. policy during the war is described as a mixture of:
Values (democracy, open trade) combined with interests (preventing a hostile hegemon).
L2S4: In 1942–1944, what was the U.S. role in the Anglo-American partnership?
Junior partner, deferring to British strategy (North Africa first)
Britain had more experience and intelligence assets, though the U.S. was out-producing everyone.
By D-Day (June 1944), the U.S. had become:
The senior partner, with numerically dominant forces and commanders like Eisenhower
This shift set the stage for the U.S. to lead postwar reconstruction.
L2S5: What share of world industrial production did the U.S. have in 1945?
It also had half the world's wealth, the largest navy and the atomic bomb.
What kind of international system emerged after 1945?
Bipolar: U.S.-centred West vs. Soviet-controlled East
The USSR was economically shattered but militarily dominant in Eastern Europe.
L2S6: must return it after the war
Soviet military presence in Eastern Europe translated into communist control.
L2S7: What did Roosevelt need from Stalin at Yalta?
Soviet entry into the Pacific war and cooperation in the UN
German reparations
Control of Poland
Access to the Bosporus
This constrained Roosevelt's leverage over Eastern Europe.
Who represented Britain by the end of Potsdam?
Attlee (replacing Churchill)
Eden
Chamberlain
Macmillan
Roosevelt had died (Truman took a tougher line) and Churchill was replaced by Attlee.
Why was administering liberated countries so contentious?
The USSR imposed communist regimes while the West expected democratic self-determination
The U.S. wanted to annex them
Britain refused to withdraw troops
All sides agreed but lacked money
Military control on the ground determined political outcomes.
Which was a sticking point at Potsdam?
Poland's borders
The Suez Canal
The Atlantic Charter
The Marshall Plan
Also Germany's future, reparations and the fate of Eastern Europe.
L2S8: According to Cox & Kennedy-Pipe, the Marshall Plan was:
Multipurpose — rebuild Europe, prevent communist gains, reconcile France and Germany
Purely humanitarian
Mainly a military alliance
Aimed at the Soviet Union's recovery
Revisionists add it helped institutionalise the East–West divide.
What is Sloan's 'Transatlantic Bargain'?
U.S. provides protection; Europe accepts U.S. leadership and alignment
Europe pays the U.S. for defence
The U.S. joins the EEC
Europe leaves NATO in exchange for aid
It was an unwritten deal that stabilised Western Europe.
Which of Lundestad's five motives for supporting integration was MOST important?
Containing Germany
The American model
A more rational, efficient Europe
Reducing the American burden
Germany had to be strong but controlled; integration 'bound' it to the West.
Lundestad's five motives in order from least to most important are:
American model → rational Europe → reducing burden → containing USSR → containing Germany
Containing Germany → containing USSR → rational Europe → burden → model
Burden → model → Germany → USSR → rational Europe
USSR → Germany → model → burden → rational Europe
Memorise the order: model, efficiency, burden, Soviets, Germany.
What did the U.S. oppose regarding European integration?
Europe as an independent 'third force' between Washington and Moscow
Any economic cooperation
The creation of the OEEC
German membership in NATO
Integration had to stay within an Atlantic framework.
Lundestad's phrase for Europe voluntarily entering a U.S.-led order is:
Empire by invitation
Empire of liberty
Imperial overstretch
Pax Britannica
Europe welcomed U.S. power because it ensured security, recovery and reconciliation.
L2S9: Why did Europe accept American leadership after WWII, unlike after WWI?
It understood the alternatives: devastation, Soviet domination or violent nationalism
This is the 'empire by invitation' dynamic.
Which institution sequence reflects European integration growth?
The war created both necessity and opportunity for these institutions.

L1S1: The whole course is about one relationship: the U.S. and Europe. This first lecture asks a basic question — why does America treat Europe the way it does? The answer starts long before NATO. Americans came from Europe and took its ideas, but they also crossed an ocean to get away from it. So America has always felt both 'family' and 'outsider' toward Europe.

Lecture 1 gives you three 'lenses' (Realism, Liberalism, Idealism) that you'll use for every later topic. When an exam question asks 'why did the U.S. do X?', you can almost always answer with one or more of these lenses. Think of this lecture as the toolkit, not just history.
America = Europe's child who moved across the ocean.
L1S2: America felt culturally European (language, law, political ideas from Britain), but geographically separate. The ocean was a shield. That meant America could choose: get involved in Europe's fights, or stay out. 'Off-shore Europe' means: part of the European family, but living on an island far away.

This explains a pattern you'll see again and again: the U.S. swings between engagement (WWI, WWII, NATO) and withdrawal (after WWI, rejecting the League). Distance gave America the luxury of choice — something European countries, stuck next to each other, never had.
The ocean gave America a choice Europe never had.
L1S3: There are three ways of thinking about U.S. foreign policy. Idealism: America is a moral example and should spread democracy and freedom ('city upon a hill'). Realism: forget morals — it's about power, security and making sure no single enemy controls Europe. Liberalism: a mix — use rules, trade and international institutions to keep peace, because democracies that trade together don't fight.

Real U.S. policy is almost never just one of these. The Marshall Plan, for example, was liberal (trade, cooperation), realist (stop communism) and idealist (help free peoples) all at once. Strong exam answers show how the lenses combine rather than picking just one.
Idealism = values. Realism = power. Liberalism = rules + trade.
L1S4: When George Washington retired (1796), he told Americans: trade with everyone, but don't tie yourself into permanent military alliances with European countries. The young U.S. was weak, and Europe's great powers were always at war — joining them would drag America into conflicts that weren't its own.

This 'no entangling alliances' rule guided America for over 150 years. That's why NATO in 1949 is such a huge deal: it was America's first permanent peacetime alliance — literally breaking Washington's advice. Whenever you see 'end of isolationism', compare it back to this speech.
Washington: trade yes, alliances no.
L1S5: In 1750 or 1800 America was a small, unimportant economy. During the 1800s it industrialised massively — factories, railways, steel, huge population growth. By 1914, according to historian Paul Kennedy's numbers, the U.S. economy was bigger than Germany and Britain combined.

Power follows money and factories. Isolationism was easy when America was weak; once it became an economic giant, it had both the ability and the interests (markets, trade routes) to act globally. This economic rise is what later let America 'rescue' Europe in two world wars and lead the West.
L1S6: In 1898 the USS Maine blew up in Havana harbour, Americans blamed Spain, and the U.S. went to war. America won easily and took Spain's colonies: the Philippines, Guam and Puerto Rico (and annexed Hawaii around the same time). Suddenly America had overseas territories and naval bases.

This is the moment America stops being only a continental power and starts acting globally — the 'Rise to Globalism'. Motives mixed: trade, naval strategy (Mahan said great powers need sea power and bases), ideology (spreading 'civilisation') and public pressure. It's the first crack in Washington's isolationism.
L1S7: The U.S. stayed neutral in WWI at first, but joined in 1917 because German submarines sank ships and Germany tried to get Mexico to attack the U.S. (Zimmermann Telegram). President Wilson wanted more than victory: a new world order with a League of Nations, self-determination and no more power politics. But the U.S. Senate refused to join the League.

Wilson is idealism in action — and its failure. Without the U.S., the League was weak and Europe's peace was unstable. Americans later concluded that walking away in 1919 helped cause WWII. That lesson is why after 1945 the U.S. did the opposite: stayed, built institutions, and joined alliances.
Wilson dreamed big; the Senate said no.
L1S8: Between the wars America pulled back: passed Neutrality Acts to stay out of wars, focused on the Great Depression at home. Meanwhile Europe fell apart — economic collapse, fascism in Germany, Italy and Spain, and the Versailles peace collapsing. Americans thought they could stay safe behind the ocean.

This period is the 'what not to do' example for later U.S. leaders. They learned that economic collapse breeds extremism, that dictators fill power vacuums, and that isolation doesn't protect you. Every post-1945 policy — Marshall Plan, NATO, the UN — is partly a reaction to this failure.
Interwar = the lesson the U.S. never wanted to repeat.
L1S9: This section puts the three lenses to work. Realism explains why the U.S. fought two world wars, contained the USSR and built NATO (keep the balance of power). Liberalism explains the Marshall Plan, UN, IMF, World Bank and support for EU integration (cooperation and trade). Idealism explains the democracy talk, human rights and belief in American exceptionalism.

The big takeaway: America is both pragmatic and moralistic at the same time. Europe is both a partner (shared values) and a tool of strategy (a buffer against threats). This dual nature is why the relationship survives crises — there are several reasons holding it together, not just one.
Power + rules + values = U.S. policy toward Europe.
L1S10: The transatlantic relationship didn't just appear in 1945. It grew out of shared culture, a long habit of staying out and then jumping in, America's economic rise, and the competition between the three lenses.
For the exam, this is your framing paragraph: whenever you write about WWII, NATO or the Cold War, you can link it back to these deep patterns — the cycle of war, retreat and re-engagement.
The roots are older than NATO.
L2S1: WWII changed everything. America came out of it not just as a winner, but as the country that would design the new world — with the biggest economy, bases everywhere, confidence in its ideas, and a plan for Europe.

This is the birth of 'American grand strategy': a long-term plan combining power (NATO), money (Marshall Plan) and institutions (EU integration). Lundestad, Cox & Kennedy-Pipe and Sloan each explain one piece of that plan.
1945: from player to designer of the system.
L2S2: When war broke out in 1939, Americans really didn't want to fight again — the Neutrality Acts and the Depression kept them home. Roosevelt knew this, so he moved slowly. In his fireside chat he said: we can be neutral by law, but I can't ask you to be neutral in your heart. Churchill meanwhile openly begged for America to come and save Europe.

Roosevelt was preparing public opinion step by step — first sympathy, then aid (Lend-Lease), then war. This shows how domestic politics limits foreign policy: even a president who sees the danger can't jump in until the public is ready.
FDR: neutral in law, not in heart.
L2S3: In August 1941 (before the U.S. was even at war) Roosevelt and Churchill signed the Atlantic Charter: no land grabs, self-determination, free trade, collective security. Then in December 1941 Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, Germany declared war on the U.S., and isolationism collapsed overnight.

The Atlantic Charter is basically the blueprint for the post-war liberal order (UN, free trade, self-determination). Pearl Harbor gave the political green light to build it. Together they show the mix of idealism (values) and realism (stop any one power dominating Europe or Asia).
Charter = the plan. Pearl Harbor = the trigger.
L2S4: At first (1942–44) the U.S. let Britain lead — Britain had more experience, so the Allies did 'North Africa first' as the British wanted. But American factories were out-producing everyone. By D-Day in 1944, American troops and generals (Eisenhower) were in charge.

This power shift inside the alliance matters: whoever leads the war leads the peace. Because America became senior partner, it — not Britain — got to shape occupation, reconstruction and the new institutions after 1945.
L2S5: In 1945 the U.S. had two-thirds of the world's industry, half its wealth, the largest navy and the only atomic bomb. Europe was in ruins. The only other big power, the USSR, was badly damaged but had a huge army sitting in Eastern Europe. So the world split into two camps — bipolarity.

Massive power meant massive choice: the U.S. could set the rules. And because the USSR controlled the East, the world became a two-way contest. Almost everything in Lectures 3–7 flows from this U.S.–Soviet split.
L2S6: Stalin said: whoever's army occupies a territory gets to impose their own system on it. So wherever the Red Army stood at the end of the war (Poland, Hungary, etc.), communism followed.

This one quote explains the division of Europe. It wasn't decided mainly at conference tables — it was decided by where armies were standing. That's why the West's promises of 'free elections' in the East couldn't be enforced.
Where the army stands, the system follows.
L2S7: At Yalta (Feb 1945) Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin tried to plan the peace — but they meant different things by 'free elections'. Roosevelt needed Stalin's help against Japan and in the UN, so he compromised. At Potsdam (July 1945) Roosevelt was dead, Truman was tougher, Churchill was replaced by Attlee, and trust was falling. They argued about Germany, Poland's borders and reparations.

These conferences show the alliance cracking. The real problem: the USSR wanted friendly (controlled) governments for security, the West wanted democratic self-determination. Those goals couldn't both be true — so cooperation turned into Cold War.
Same words, different meanings: 'free elections'.
L2S8: Three authors, three tools. Cox & Kennedy-Pipe: the Marshall Plan rebuilt Europe but also stopped communism and helped divide East and West. Sloan: NATO is a 'transatlantic bargain' — the U.S. protects Europe, Europe accepts U.S. leadership. Lundestad: the U.S. pushed European integration for five reasons, the most important being to keep Germany under control. Europe accepted all this willingly — 'empire by invitation'.

This is probably the most exam-heavy section. Learn: (1) Marshall Plan = economic tool, partly blamed for dividing Europe; (2) NATO = security bargain; (3) Lundestad's 5 motives in order, with Germany as #1; (4) the U.S. wanted a united Europe, but never an independent 'third force'. 'Empire by invitation' means U.S. power was asked for, not imposed.
Money (Marshall) + protection (NATO) + integration (Lundestad) = the U.S. strategy.
L2S9: WWII created all the conditions for U.S. leadership: America was rich while Europe was destroyed; fascism made democracy feel urgent; the Soviet threat pushed the West together; and there was a chance to build new institutions (UN, Bretton Woods, NATO, OEEC → EU). Unlike after WWI, Europe now wanted the U.S. to stay.

The key difference from 1919: this time, Europe invited America in, because the alternatives were ruin, Soviet control or another round of nationalism. And the U.S. accepted that European security = American security. That's why the U.S. never left again.
After 1945, Europe said 'please stay' — and America did.
L2S10: After WWII, the U.S. became the West's indispensable power, rebuilt Europe inside a U.S.-led system, faced the USSR in a two-bloc world, and tied itself to Europe through institutions.
Use this as your conclusion template: WWII → U.S. dominance → containment of USSR + integration of Germany + open markets → long-lasting transatlantic community (NATO, EU, liberal order).
WWII = birth certificate of the transatlantic community.
L3S1: In just five years (1945–1950), the U.S. went from 'let's bring the troops home' to 'we will defend Western Europe permanently'. It launched the Marshall Plan and created NATO. This wasn't planned from the start — it happened because fear of the Soviets grew and wartime cooperation collapsed.

The key word is 'not inevitable'. Exam answers should show it was a step-by-step reaction to events (Soviet moves, British weakness, European requests), explained by four authors: Offner (Truman's mindset), Cox & Kennedy-Pipe (economics), Lundestad (integration), Sloan (NATO).
L3S2: In 1945 the U.S. was by far the strongest country, but it didn't know what to do. It had three pulls at once: go home (the public wanted demobilisation), keep cooperating with the Soviets, or fear that a ruined Europe would fall to communism. Offner says Truman started confused, moralistic, and only slowly accepted confrontation.
This shows that strength doesn't automatically mean a clear strategy. The early Truman years were improvisation. The Cold War strategy came later, as a response — not as a master plan.
L3S3: After 1945 there were two superpowers, but they were very different. The U.S. was rich and untouched at home. The USSR had lost about 10% of its population and was economically wrecked — but its army was huge and sat in Eastern Europe. Britain had become a 'junior partner' that could no longer afford a global role.

The Soviets were strong and scared at the same time — after being invaded twice, they wanted buffer states. The U.S. saw those buffers as expansion. This mismatch of perceptions (security vs. aggression) is why the Cold War began in Europe.
USSR: strong army, broken economy, deep fear.
L3S4: At Yalta the Allies agreed to divide Germany, the Soviets promised free elections, and Stalin agreed to join the UN and fight Japan. By Potsdam, things got worse: Truman (confident thanks to the atomic bomb) was tougher, and no one agreed on reparations, Germany or Poland.

Behind the polite agreements were two incompatible visions: U.S. = democracy and open markets; USSR = 'friendly' (controlled) governments. Offner stresses Truman deeply distrusted Stalin. And the Red Army on the ground decided the outcome in the East.
L3S5: U.S. planners knew Europe mattered — its collapse had helped cause WWII. But there was huge pressure to leave: the Pacific war, 'bring the boys home', an isolationist Congress. Lundestad and Offner both say that in 1945–46 the U.S. was hesitant and hoped Europeans would handle their own problems.
This sets up the big contrast: in 1945 no one imagined a permanent U.S. presence in Europe. By 1949 it existed. The change came from events, not from initial intentions.
Knew Europe mattered — still wanted to leave.
L3S6: In 1946–47 the Soviets did a series of things that alarmed Washington: set up communist puppet governments in Eastern Europe, pressured Turkey and demanded passage through the Bosporus straits, backed Greek communists, refused to leave northern Iran, and Stalin gave a speech in 1946 calling capitalism and communism incompatible.

Each move on its own was regional, but together Americans saw a global, ideological plan. This is the turning point from 'cooperate' to 'contain'. Greece and Turkey especially matter because they led directly to the Truman Doctrine.
1946–47: the list that turned allies into rivals.
L3S7: George Kennan, a U.S. diplomat in Moscow, wrote the Long Telegram (1946) and the 'X Article' (1947). His message: the USSR will keep expanding because of fear and ideology, but it can be stopped — not by war, but by firm, patient 'containment' using economic and political strength. Western Europe, the industrial heart of the world, must not be lost.

Containment became THE U.S. strategy for the whole Cold War. Note Kennan's original idea was mostly economic and political (Marshall Plan style), not military — the military version came later with NSC-68.
Kennan: don't fight them, contain them.
L3S8: In March 1947 Britain told the U.S. it couldn't afford to support Greece and Turkey anymore. Truman went to Congress and said America must support 'free peoples' resisting subjugation. The U.S. took over Britain's role.

This is the real break with Washington's 1796 advice: the U.S. formally promised to intervene abroad to stop communism. It also turned the Cold War into a moral, global battle — free world vs. totalitarianism — which fits Offner's view of Truman's moral worldview.
Truman Doctrine: America takes Britain's job.
L3S9: Containment became real action. The Marshall Plan gave $12.5 billion to Western Europe (1948–51), rebuilt economies, and made communism less attractive — the Soviets refused it, deepening the split. The CIA secretly funded anti-communist parties in Italy's 1948 election. And the U.S. made Europeans share out the aid together through the OEEC.

Notice the link: aid → required cooperation (OEEC) → early European integration. Containment and integration are two sides of the same coin. Lundestad calls the Marshall Plan the first tool of 'empire by integration'.
Money, secret help, and forced teamwork.
L3S10: Before NATO, Europeans built their own defence pacts: the Treaty of Dunkirk (1947, France + Britain), then the Brussels Pact (1948, adding Belgium, Netherlands, Luxembourg). The U.S. Senate's Vandenberg Resolution (1948) allowed America to join a peacetime alliance. NATO (1949) then wrapped all this into an Atlantic alliance.

Crucial point: Europeans asked first. They wanted U.S. guarantees against the USSR and a solution to Germany. That's Lundestad's 'empire by invitation' — American power came because Europe invited it.
Europe knocked; America answered with NATO.
L3S11: NATO's Article 5: an attack on one member is an attack on all. For the U.S. this was the first peacetime alliance since 1796 — the formal end of isolationism. It put Western Europe under the U.S. nuclear umbrella. Sloan calls it a bargain: America protects, Europe gives bases and accepts U.S. leadership. Early NATO even included non-democracies like Portugal.

Portugal shows NATO was about geopolitics (stopping the USSR) more than ideals (democracy). Also remember NATO started as just a treaty; the real military structures (SHAPE, SACEUR) came in the early 1950s after Korea.
L3S12: NSC-68 (1950) was a secret U.S. strategy paper. It said communism must be resisted everywhere, demanded a huge military build-up (including the hydrogen bomb) and treated the Cold War as global. The Korean War started the same year, which seemed to prove it right.
NSC-68 turns Kennan's limited, mostly economic containment into militarised global containment. It's the moment the Cold War becomes truly worldwide — with Europe still the central front.
NSC-68: containment goes global and military.
L3S13: Five reasons the U.S. never went back to isolation after 1950: Europe asked it to stay (Lundestad); a collapsed Europe would endanger the world economy (Cox & Kennedy-Pipe); Truman's view hardened (Offner); NATO made commitments permanent (Sloan); and Europe became the frontline of a global ideological war.

This section maps one author to one reason — perfect for an essay structure. Learn the pairings: Lundestad = invitation, Cox & Kennedy-Pipe = economics, Offner = Truman's mindset, Sloan = NATO institutions.
Four authors, four reasons, one result: no going back.
L3S14: By 1950 the U.S. had rejected isolationism, put troops in Europe permanently, adopted containment, launched the Marshall Plan, encouraged integration and created NATO. That is the birth of modern transatlantic relations.
The glue holding it together: shared interests, shared institutions, shared threats — and the belief that European and American security are the same thing.
L4S1: After WWII, Germany was the biggest question in Europe: it was the industrial heart of the continent and sat right in the middle. Every winner wanted something different — France wanted safety from Germany, the USSR wanted a buffer and control, the U.S. wanted a stable rebuilt economy, Britain wanted balance. Those goals couldn't fit together, so Germany ended up split.

'Structural, not accidental' is the key phrase: no one sat down and decided to divide Germany forever. The clash of interests made it almost unavoidable. From 1945 to 1961 temporary occupation zones slowly hardened into two countries, and Berlin became the Cold War's hottest spot.
Whoever got Germany would tip the balance — so nobody could let the other have it.
L4S2: Germany in 1945 was destroyed: cities flattened, millions homeless, hunger, no government (Bessel). The Allies agreed on the '4 Ds' — demilitarise, denazify, decartelise (break up big industrial groups), democratise. But they disagreed on the big stuff: one central Germany or a decentralised one? Rebuild its industry or shrink it? Unified and neutral, or split?

Agreement on punishing the past was easy; agreement on building the future was impossible. France wanted Germany weak, the USSR wanted control or neutrality, and the U.S. slowly moved toward rebuilding. That gap is where division started.
Agreed on the 4 Ds, disagreed on everything else.
L4S3: Everyone feared Germany, but differently. France had been invaded three times (1870, 1914, 1940), so it wanted Germany weak, the Ruhr's coal and steel under international control, maybe even permanent partition (Creswell & Trachtenberg). The USSR had been invaded twice through Germany, so it wanted reparations and a friendly socialist Germany. The U.S. feared a collapsed Germany would go communist, so it switched from punishing (Morgenthau Plan) to rebuilding.

The U.S. logic (Kennan): Germany must be strong enough to resist communism but locked inside Western institutions so it can't threaten anyone again. This 'strong but controlled' idea returns in Lecture 6 as the #1 reason the U.S. supported European integration.
France: weak Germany. USSR: friendly Germany. U.S.: strong-but-anchored Germany.
L4S4: Step by step, cooperation broke down. The Allied Control Council needed everyone to agree, so it froze. The U.S. and UK merged their zones (Bizonia, then Trizonia with France). Stalin rejected the Marshall Plan. In 1948 the West introduced a new currency, the Deutsche Mark; the Soviets answered by blockading West Berlin. The West flew in supplies for almost a year — the Berlin Airlift — and won.

The Airlift was a huge symbolic win: it proved the West wouldn't abandon Berlin and made Germans see the Americans as protectors rather than occupiers. Kempe highlights General Clay proving the doubters wrong.
New money → blockade → airlift → West wins hearts.
L4S5: In 1949 two German states were born: the Federal Republic (West Germany, FRG) in May — a parliamentary democracy led by Adenauer, tied to the West; and the Democratic Republic (East Germany, GDR) in October — a Soviet-controlled one-party state that people kept fleeing.

Division became permanent because the two systems were incompatible, the Cold War deepened, each joined an opposing alliance (NATO 1949 / Warsaw Pact 1955), and their economies split — West boomed (Wirtschaftswunder), East stagnated.
L4S6: Berlin was a Western island inside East Germany. West Berlin had Allied troops, was linked to West Germany's economy, and showcased Western freedom. That made it an escape door: more than 2.5 million East Germans fled through it between 1949 and 1961, many of them skilled workers.

Every person who left was an embarrassment for communism and a loss for the GDR economy. That's why Berlin was 'the most dangerous place': the East had to stop the flow, and the West had promised to defend the city.
West Berlin = the open door out of communism.
L4S7: Coleman explains Eisenhower's thinking in the 1950s: Berlin is a test of credibility — look weak and the Soviets will push harder. But he didn't want a war either. Instead of building big conventional armies, he relied on nuclear deterrence ('massive retaliation') and detailed plans for blockades or harassment of convoys.
The balancing act: firm enough to deter, careful enough not to start WWIII. This 'hold Berlin but avoid war on bad terms' logic continues under Kennedy.
Ike: hold Berlin, threaten nukes, avoid war.
L4S8: France kept trying to keep Germany weak and limited — internationalise the Ruhr, decentralise, keep occupation rights. It also worried the U.S. was rebuilding Germany too fast and might favour Germany over France.

This French pressure slowed German sovereignty, shaped NATO, and influenced the European Defence Community debate (which France itself later killed — see Lecture 6). It's a reminder that the U.S. had to manage its allies' fears, not just the Soviets.
France kept its hand on the brake.
L4S9: From 1958 Khrushchev demanded the West renegotiate Berlin's status, threatening to sign a separate treaty with East Germany and cut Western access. His reasons: East Germany was bleeding people and near collapse, and he wanted to test U.S. leaders. The U-2 spy plane shot down in 1960 wrecked a summit. Kennedy in 1961 sounded tough in public but was privately unsure and wanted to avoid escalation — Moscow read that as weakness.
This crisis shows how Berlin connected local problems (refugees) to superpower prestige. Kempe's view of Kennedy as hesitant is important: perceived weakness can invite pressure.
Khrushchev pushed because East Germany was emptying.
L4S10: On 13 August 1961 East Germany sealed the border and built the Berlin Wall to stop people fleeing. Khrushchev approved it as the 'lesser evil' — better than losing East Germany, and it avoided a direct fight with the U.S. Kennedy was shocked but relieved: 'a wall is better than a war'. In October U.S. and Soviet tanks stood face to face at Checkpoint Charlie until the Soviets pulled back first.

The Wall was brutal, but it actually stabilised the crisis — the refugee drain stopped, and both sides avoided war. Checkpoint Charlie shows how close things came. The Wall became the symbol of a divided Europe for 28 years.
A wall instead of a war.
L4S11: After 1961 things settled into a frozen pattern: East Germany firmly Soviet, West Germany firmly in NATO, Berlin no longer an escape route. Two Germanies became normal.
The Wall didn't end the Cold War — it just removed its most urgent crisis. Stability came at the price of permanent division.
L4S12: Germany defined the Cold War because it was Europe's economic centre, its alignment decided the balance of power, it embodied communism vs. democracy, Berlin symbolised freedom vs. control, and both blocs feared a united Germany joining the other side.
Division 'solved' the post-war problem (no side got all of Germany) but created long-term confrontation — until the Wall fell in 1989 and Germany reunited in 1990.
Germany: the Cold War's centre of gravity.
L5S1: This lecture is about the end of European empires (Britain, France, the Netherlands) and America's role in it. The U.S. had no big colonial empire of its own to lose, but it shaped the outcome by changing what the world considered acceptable, by pressuring its allies, and by viewing everything through the Cold War. Hopkins' big idea: after 1945 the world economy changed so much that owning territory stopped making sense.

The guiding questions in this section are basically your possible exam questions: What did the U.S. think of empires? How did WWII change that? How hard did it push Britain and France? How did the Cold War change things? Why did the U.S. and UK clash over Suez in 1956?
Empires ended because they stopped paying — and stopped being acceptable.
L5S2: Before WWII, European countries ruled much of the world through military power, economic extraction, racist 'civilising mission' ideas, control of trade routes and laws that kept colonised people subordinate. Hobsbawm stresses it wasn't just armies: capitalism, industry and control of world markets made Europe dominant.
This is the 'before' picture. It looked permanent — until WWII shattered the money, the power and the moral justification behind it.
Empire ran on guns, money and racist ideas.
L5S3: Two kinds of reasons empires ended. Material: Europe was broke after WWII, colonial wars (Malaya, Kenya, Indochina, Algeria) cost too much, and in a globalised economy you could trade and invest without ruling territory. Non-material: colonised peoples demanded independence (nationalism), human rights and the UN made colonialism look illegitimate, and Europeans who had just suffered Nazi occupation found it harder to justify occupying others.
Exams love 'material vs. non-material' distinctions — learn three of each. Hopkins argues both changed together: the economic logic and the moral logic of empire collapsed at the same time.
Couldn't afford it, couldn't justify it.
L5S4: America said it was anti-colonial (it was born fighting an empire), but in practice it ran colonies (the Philippines) and backed friendly dictators in Latin America. FDR's line about the Dominican dictator Trujillo — 'he's a SOB, but he's our SOB' — sums it up.

This contradiction runs through the whole lecture: U.S. anti-imperial talk vs. self-interested practice (Louis). Hopkins adds that the U.S. went through its own decolonisation of the Philippines, Puerto Rico and Hawaii after 1945.
Anti-empire in words, self-interest in deeds.
L5S5: Many Americans disliked the British Empire — undemocratic and closed to U.S. trade. Life Magazine (1942) told Britain: we're not fighting to keep your empire together. Churchill shot back that he didn't become Prime Minister to dismantle the empire. Roosevelt saw empire as outdated and immoral — but LaFeber shows he also wanted to weaken British influence and open markets for America.
Idealism and self-interest pointed the same way here: ending empires was moral and good for U.S. business. This tension between the two closest allies foreshadows Suez in 1956.
FDR vs. Churchill: the empire fight inside the alliance.
L5S6: India's independence (1947) was the turning point. The Quit India movement showed mass support for independence; Britain was too poor for a long war; it feared civil war and mutiny; and the U.S. pushed for self-determination. Once India — the 'jewel' and economic keystone of the empire — was gone, the rest of the empire's logic fell apart.

Britain then tried to manage decline: keep influence through the Commonwealth and later Europe instead of direct rule. Washington saw Indian independence as stabilising Asia and making communism less attractive.
Lose India, lose the empire's reason to exist.
L5S7: After 1947 the U.S. cared more about stopping communism than ending colonialism. So it behaved inconsistently: it pressured the Dutch to leave Indonesia (1945–49) but then supported France in Indochina because the Vietnamese independence movement was communist.

This is the key shift: Idealism → Containment. Hopkins says the Cold War often froze or distorted decolonisation, because both superpowers competed for influence over new states. When an exam asks 'why was U.S. policy inconsistent?', this is the answer.
Anti-colonial — unless the rebels were communist.
L5S8: During WWII Roosevelt thought France shouldn't get Indochina (Vietnam) back and proposed an international trusteeship. But Churchill opposed it (fearing a precedent for British colonies), China's Chiang didn't want the job, and the State Department wanted a strong France for Europe. By 1945 FDR dropped the idea — France returned, leading to the First Indochina War (1946–54). In Algeria, France fought a brutal war; Eisenhower and Dulles valued France as a NATO ally but quietly pushed for a negotiated solution.

Indochina shows how European needs (a strong France vs. the USSR) beat anti-colonial principles. Algeria shows colonial wars became politically impossible once world opinion turned against them (Hopkins, Hobsbawm).
Europe first, principles second — Indochina.
L5S9: In 1956 Egypt's leader Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal. Britain and France, with Israel, secretly planned an invasion to take it back. Eisenhower was furious: they had deceived him, it looked like old-style imperialism, and it could push Arab states toward Moscow. The U.S. backed a UN ceasefire and refused to support the British pound, forcing Britain and France to retreat in humiliation.

Suez is the biggest transatlantic rupture of the post-war era. It proved Britain could no longer act as an independent global power without the U.S. (Louis). Britain drew the lesson: stick close to America and move toward Europe (Lundestad). France drew the opposite lesson: don't trust America (leads to de Gaulle, Lecture 7). Nasser became an anti-colonial hero.
Suez: the day America pulled the plug on the British Empire.
L5S10: 'Out-of-area' means problems outside NATO's European zone — the Middle East, Asia, Africa — that still matter for Western security and resources. Europeans wanted to keep influence and trade with former colonies. The U.S. talked anti-colonialism but in practice wanted stability, feared nationalism could help communists, and accepted informal (neo-colonial) control.

Pattern to remember: U.S. pressure + Cold War + European weakness forced empires to end, but new dependencies (aid, security deals, economic influence) replaced them. Hopkins calls this a new post-colonial globalisation — informal control instead of formal empire.
Formal empire out, informal influence in.
L5S11: By the late 1950s Britain and France had lost most of their empires, and the U.S. had become the main Western power in Africa, Asia and the Middle East. NATO now had to decide whether and how to act outside Europe.
Lundestad: the shift from empire to partnership — America replaced European empires not by ruling colonies, but through alliances, economic integration and leadership.
America replaced the empires — without becoming one.
L6S1: Normally great powers want their rivals divided. The U.S. did the opposite: it actively pushed Western Europe to unite economically and politically, and accepted institutions above national governments — even though a united Europe could one day compete with America. Lundestad calls this 'empire by integration': U.S. influence came through aid, pressure, security guarantees and economic weight, not conquest.

The core question for this lecture: why and how did the U.S. promote European integration (1945–late 1960s)? Answer: because it served U.S. interests — containing the USSR, managing Germany, rebuilding markets — as long as Europe stayed inside the Atlantic (NATO) framework.
The only great power that helped its partners unite.
L6S2: The idea of a united Europe is older than 1945: interwar movements like Pan-Europa and the Briand plan, even Hitler's twisted vision of a Europe under German domination, and Churchill's 1946 call for a 'United States of Europe'. None worked before, because the conditions weren't there.

WWII created the conditions: Europe was ruined, old powers exhausted, Germany needed to be re-integrated, the USSR was a new threat — and the U.S. was powerful enough to push, while Europeans were ready to listen.
L6S3: America needed Europe to be rich, because rich Europeans buy American goods. As one U.S. official put it, foreigners can't buy from you unless they're producing and selling too. Fragmented European economies with tariffs everywhere were inefficient, couldn't absorb U.S. exports and were politically unstable.

Integration = economic common sense: bigger markets, fewer barriers, economies of scale — and a way to let Germany's economy recover without scaring its neighbours. A united Europe fitted America's global economic plans.
A rich Europe = a customer for America.
L6S4: Marshall said the plan targeted 'hunger, poverty, desperation and chaos', not any country. But it was also strategic. The U.S. insisted Europeans manage the aid together through the OEEC — so they had to plan jointly and share data. Integration started as a condition for getting money. It also became part of containment: prosperous countries resist communism, and aid kept France and Italy from drifting left.

The Marshall Plan strengthened pro-integration leaders like Monnet and Schuman and kick-started the Western 'economic miracle'. It's the bridge between Lecture 3 (containment) and Lecture 6 (integration).
L6S5: Five reasons the U.S. wanted European integration (Lundestad): (1) a federal Europe looked like America; (2) bigger markets meant a stronger capitalist partner; (3) Europe could eventually carry more of its own burden; (4) a united Europe was a stronger barrier against the USSR; (5) MOST IMPORTANT: integration solved the 'German problem' — Germany could be strong but tied down, and France could accept German recovery because shared institutions diluted German power.
If you remember one thing: Germany is the decisive motive. Also note the burden complaint — every president from Truman to Johnson grumbled that Europeans weren't 'doing enough'.
Integration's #1 job: make a strong Germany safe.
L6S6: Britain stayed out of early integration. It felt it had won the war, still had an empire and a global role, and didn't want to give power to supranational bodies. Churchill liked European unity — for others. Britain refused to join the coal and steel community (1952), dismissed the Messina talks that led to the EEC, and created EFTA (1960) as a looser alternative.
The U.S. wanted Britain inside the EEC to balance France and Germany and to keep Europe Atlantic-minded. That's why de Gaulle's vetoes of British entry (1963, 1967) frustrated Washington so much.
L6S7: First steps: the Benelux customs union (1948) proved small-scale integration worked. The European Coal and Steel Community (1952) put France and Germany's coal and steel — the raw materials of war — under shared control, making war between them practically impossible (Monnet and Schuman's idea; strongly backed by the U.S.). The European Defence Community, a planned joint army, failed in 1954 when France itself voted it down, despite U.S. pressure.
ECSC = success through economics; EDC = failure in defence. After the EDC collapsed, defence stayed in NATO and integration continued on the economic track.
Coal and steel worked; a European army didn't.
L6S8: The Treaty of Rome (1957) created the European Economic Community (common market) and EURATOM (atomic energy). Britain stayed out again, preferring EFTA. The EEC's common tariff discriminated against U.S. goods, but the U.S. accepted it because political unity was worth more than short-term trade losses — and it hoped global GATT talks would lower tariffs anyway.
This shows U.S. priorities clearly: strategy over economics. America paid an economic price for a politically stronger, more stable Western Europe.
America accepted losing some trade to gain a united ally.
L6S9: The U.S. had one firm condition: European integration must happen inside the Atlantic framework, with NATO on top. Europe should cooperate with America, not become a separate power centre or a neutral 'third force'.
This single rule explains U.S. attitudes to everything else: wanting Britain in, opposing de Gaulle's independent Europe, insisting on NATO leadership. Integrate Europe — but don't create a rival.
Unite, but stay under the Atlantic umbrella.
L6S10: De Gaulle challenged the U.S. vision. He vetoed Britain's EEC entry twice (1963, 1967), calling it an American 'Trojan horse'. He pulled France out of NATO's integrated military command (1966). And he wanted a 'Europe of Nations' — cooperation between sovereign states, not a strong supranational Commission.

The U.S. didn't fight him head-on. It stayed calm, built closer ties with West Germany and the European Commission, and kept supporting a supranational Europe. Lecture 7 goes much deeper into de Gaulle.
De Gaulle: Europe yes, American Europe no.
L6S11: Historian Guderzo pushes back on the idea that Lyndon Johnson ignored Europe because of Vietnam. LBJ said he spent a lot of time on European issues: complaints of neglect, burden-sharing in NATO, Britain's economic weakness, tension with de Gaulle, and the Kennedy Round trade talks. By 1967 there was 'cautious optimism': Germany stable, France recovering, Britain under Wilson ready to join.
LBJ kept supporting integration — on the usual condition that it stayed Atlantic-oriented and strengthened Western unity. A good 'revisionist' point for essays.
L6S12: Big picture: the U.S. was the most important outside force behind European integration. Its motives were strategic (containment, Germany), economic (markets) and ideological (the American model). But support had limits: Europe had to stay in NATO and not become an independent bloc.

The U.S. was both architect (it pushed integration) and constraint (it set the boundaries). De Gaulle was the biggest challenge, yet support continued. Integration depended on America but also slowly rebalanced the partnership.
Architect and fence at the same time.
L7S1: By the 1960s Western Europe was richer, more confident and less willing to just follow America — helped by economic recovery, colonial crises, nuclear weapons and U.S. distraction in Vietnam. The loudest challenger was French President Charles de Gaulle, who wanted France to be an independent world power again and less dominated by the U.S. and Britain.
This lecture is about a problem inside the Western camp: an ally, not an enemy, questioning American leadership.
L7S2: In 1955 the Paris Accords let West Germany rearm and join NATO — a high point of Western unity. Then Suez (1956) changed everything: the U.S. forced Britain and France to retreat. France concluded America was too dominant and started distancing itself; Britain concluded it must stay close to America. Both built their own nuclear weapons. Meanwhile Eisenhower complained that Europeans took U.S. money, ignored U.S. advice and then criticised the U.S.
Same event, opposite lessons: Suez pushed London toward Washington and Paris away from it. Burden-sharing (who pays for defence) also becomes a lasting irritant.
Suez: Britain moved closer, France moved away.
L7S3: Nuclear weapons became a source of tension. Britain had the bomb (1953, per the guide) and renewed nuclear cooperation with the U.S. in 1958. France tested its own bomb in 1960 — the force de frappe. The U.S. proposed a Multilateral Nuclear Force (MLF) to give West Germany some controlled nuclear role, but de Gaulle opposed it and it failed.

De Gaulle saw the MLF as a U.S. trick to keep control of Europe, block France from becoming Europe's main nuclear power, and possibly empower Germany. For him, real independence meant your own national bomb, not sharing America's.
L7S4: De Gaulle believed France was a great nation that had lost its rightful place. He thought the U.S. and Britain formed an 'Anglo-Saxon bloc' that sidelined France, and that Europe should be led by continental powers — 'a Europe from the Atlantic to the Urals', free from superpower domination. His bad experience with Roosevelt during WWII convinced him America would always want to dominate.
Understanding his worldview explains all his moves: the bomb, the vetoes on Britain, leaving NATO's command, talking to Moscow. It's about grandeur and independence.
L7S5: De Gaulle left NATO's military side step by step: 1959 pulled the Mediterranean fleet from NATO command; 1963 the Atlantic fleet; 1964 refused the Test Ban Treaty; then in March 1966 left the integrated military command entirely. All NATO troops had to leave France by 1967 and NATO's headquarters moved to Brussels. France stayed in NATO politically.

Why: nuclear sovereignty, freedom to act as a mediator between East and West, keeping Germany from gaining nuclear influence, and refusing U.S. dominance. It was NATO's first big structural crisis since 1949.
Step by step out of the command — but not out of NATO.
L7S6: Some U.S. officials wanted to confront France, but Johnson chose a calm, patient approach: keep the other 14 members united and don't give de Gaulle a propaganda win. NATO reorganised: the Defence Planning Committee became the main military body (without France), HQ moved to Brussels, and the Nuclear Planning Group gave West Germany and others a say in nuclear planning without giving them weapons. The Harmel Report (1967) said NATO should do both deterrence AND détente (dialogue with the East).
Harmel is the clever answer to de Gaulle, who argued détente made NATO pointless. NATO said: détente is part of our job too. The alliance became political as well as military (Wenger).
Don't fight de Gaulle — adapt NATO.
L7S7: De Gaulle's goals pointed in several directions: restore French grandeur (the bomb gave symbolic equality); reduce 'Anglo-Saxon' influence (two vetoes on Britain); open to Eastern Europe and the USSR (Moscow visit 1966, per Jackson's chapter); and contain Germany, fearing its nationalism and nuclear ambitions.
Note the twist: his détente with Moscow was partly anti-German — another way to keep West Germany in check.
Grandeur, anti-Anglo-Saxon, opening East, watching Germany.
L7S8: De Gaulle openly criticised the U.S. war in Vietnam in a 1966 speech in Phnom Penh, calling it colonial-style — Americans thought this was rich coming from France. In the 1967 Middle East crisis he warned Israel not to attack, imposed an arms embargo, and made a notorious remark about the Jewish people that caused uproar. He also positioned France as a post-colonial voice for the developing world.
These global disagreements deepened U.S.–French estrangement beyond NATO itself.
De Gaulle vs. U.S. on Vietnam and the Middle East.
L7S9: May 1968's mass protests weakened de Gaulle. In 1969 he lost a referendum on constitutional reform and resigned. His successors moved France closer to NATO, toned down anti-Americanism and accepted European integration more readily.
The peak of transatlantic tension ended with him personally — showing how much one leader can shape alliance politics.
L7S10: France was a unique problem because it came from inside the Western bloc and questioned both U.S. leadership and NATO's structure, combining nationalism, nuclear independence and big ambitions. The U.S. responded by reforming NATO, consulting more, accepting more multilateral politics and avoiding a direct fight.
The surprise ending: the crisis made NATO stronger, forcing it to adapt and become both a military and a political alliance.
The troublesome ally made NATO stronger.
